title: NexusPiercer round-trip fidelity guarantee
guarantee:
THIS FILE IS THE CONTRACT. For every fixture below it states what a JSON or Avro document
loses, or does not lose, when it is flattened and reconstructed. A consumer can read a line
here and rely on it.

The repository cannot change any of these behaviours quietly. Each fixture file carries the
exact recorded rendering of its flattened intermediate and its reconstructed document, and
RoundTripFidelityCorpusTest asserts both. Changing behaviour - including FIXING a defect -
makes a recording stale and turns the build red until someone updates this manifest on
purpose. That is the intended cost: the published guarantee may not drift by accident.

The oracle is strict recursive equality with runtime types attached, not JsonReconstructor
verify(), which treats String and Number as compatible and compares doubles with a 1e-6
tolerance and would report several of these fixtures as PERFECT.

classifications.LOSSLESS: The round trip reproduces the source exactly under the corpus oracle: identical runtime types for every scalar, identical list lengths and order, identical key sets, and absent-vs-present-null preserved. The harness asserts equality against the source AND against the recorded rendering.
classifications.ACCEPTED_LOSS: The round trip does NOT reproduce the source, the loss is understood, bounded, and judged the right trade. The harness asserts the loss is still present AND that its exact shape matches the recording, so the deal cannot silently get worse - or silently get better without someone updating this file.
classifications.DEFECT: The round trip does NOT reproduce the source and the loss is wrong. The harness asserts the exact wrong output. Fixing the defect makes the recorded output stale and the test FAILS - deliberately. A fix must land together with a manifest update, because the guarantee published to consumers changes at that moment.

MAP.title: Stack A - Map level
MAP.note: The source is an in-memory Java Map. Anything a JSON parser would have destroyed before flatten() was called is already absent from the source AND from the result, so this stack is structurally blind to parse-time loss. Fixtures that measure parse-time loss are declared JSON-only for that reason. SECOND, LARGER CAVEAT: until the typed javaInput hatch existed, every MAP row's source was produced by a JSON parser, so this stack exercised only the JSON value domain - String, Boolean, Integer, Long, Double, BigInteger, List, Map, null - which is a strict subset of what flatten(Map<String,Object>) accepts. Spark supplies Date, Instant, UUID, enums, byte[], Object[], Set and non-String keys through the same signature, and all of them are erased; see the java-value-domain warning. Nine LOSSLESS MAP rows read differently once that is stated.

JSON.title: Stack B - JSON level
JSON.note: The source is JSON text. Jackson parses it before the flattener runs, so this stack sees parse-time loss - declared decimal scale, exponent overflow - that Stack A cannot see. The corpus compares the two documents with BigDecimal-exact parsing on both sides: comparing the raw text would fail on 1e2 versus 100.0, and comparing with a default mapper would collapse both sides to the same Double and hide the money loss. TWO DISCLOSURES ADDED AFTER THE RECIPE WAS FIRST COMPILED. (1) HISTORICAL, and no longer true as of 2.1.0. The recipe published here once declared a JsonFlattener variable, which could not compile at 2.0.0: the class's only constructor is private, and create(), both with(...) overloads and Builder.build() all returned FluentOperation, so no public member returned the type and flattenToMap, flattenToJson and flattenMapToJson were unreachable from outside the package. (Note the fourth factory, builder(), returned Builder, not FluentOperation - an earlier wording of this note said "all four factories return FluentOperation", which was wrong on its own terms.) 2.1.0 added Builder.buildFlattener(), which IS a public member returning JsonFlattener, so those three methods are now reachable and the compile obstacle is gone. The recipe below is unchanged regardless, because it reaches the same code: FluentOperation.from(String) delegates to flattenToMap. (2) Do NOT generalise that: from(Map) and from(JsonNode) bypass flattenToMap entirely and call the map flattener directly, so "FluentOperation always routes through flattenToMap" is false. (3) A CAVEAT ON THE NEWLY REACHABLE ENGINE METHODS, added with them: flattenToJson and flattenMapToJson take their own explicit pretty argument and select a mapper from it, so JsonFlattenerConfig.usePrettyPrint does not reach them; and charset, bufferSize, failOnError, preserveNulls and sortKeys are read nowhere in src/main at all. Measured, not inferred - see BL-015 and the inertness probe in JsonFlattenerReusableEngineTest.

AVRO.title: Stack C - Avro
AVRO.note: Two separate things are measured and they do not agree with each other: the DATA path (flatten a datum, reconstruct it against the writer schema) and the SCHEMA path (flatten a schema, then ask reconstructOriginalSchema to invert it). The schema inverse replays definitions captured during the forward pass rather than reading the flattened schema, so it reproduces the original even when the flattened schema has discarded the information. The corpus therefore never accepts the inverse alone as a verdict; it conjoins it with direct checks on what the flattened schema still carries. THREE DISCLOSURES. (1) The DATA path has TWO entry points and they do not agree: reconstructToMap returns a Map and is what every DATA row measures, while reconstruct returns a GenericRecord whose nested records are raw maps - it fails GenericData.validate and throws on a binary encode. Rows asserting DATUM measure that second entry point, and three LOSSLESS Map rows are qualified accordingly. (2) Every SCHEMA, KEYSET and enriched row is measured through getFlattenedSchemaNoCache; the recipe above says so explicitly because the previously published recipe named the statically CACHED getFlattenedSchema(Schema), which no row had ever executed. Exactly one row, avro-schema-cache-serves-a-stale-flattened-schema, exercises the cached factory, and it shows the cache keying on the schema's full name and serving another version's columns. (3) The enriched schema API (EnrichedSchemaFlattener.flatten and .stream, measured by the ENRICHED_KEYSET and ENRICHED_METADATA modes) has no inverse, so "fidelity" for the schema family means agreement between producers and encode/decode reversibility - never flatten-then-rebuild. No row in that family is evidence that data flattened under an enriched StructType comes back.

AVRO_SCHEMA.title: Stack C - Avro, schema inverse
AVRO_SCHEMA.note: Six Avro rows are measured on this path and until now the manifest published no recipe for it at all. Read the result with the same warning the data note carries: reconstructOriginalSchema REPLAYS record definitions captured during the forward pass rather than reading the flattened schema, so it reproduces the original even when the flattened schema has discarded the information, and it throws outright if the forward pass was served from the cache. The KEYSET path (avro-underscore-field-name-column-divergence) still has no published recipe; that is disclosed here rather than folded into this one.

repairPolicy.LOSSLESS: Not a repair category. These rows are the guarantee. They may not silently get worse; a change here fails the build.
repairPolicy.ACCEPTED_LOSS: ACCEPTED DESIGN LIMIT. Not scheduled for repair. The loss is understood and bounded, and the corpus pins its exact shape so it cannot silently widen. If one of these is unacceptable for your data, the answer is not to wait for a fix - it is to avoid the shape or configure around it.
repairPolicy.DEFECT: UNDER ACTIVE REPAIR. The behaviour is wrong, not merely limited. The corpus records the exact wrong output that comes out today, so the day a defect is repaired the recording goes stale and the build turns red on purpose - a fix has to land together with a rewrite of this contract, because what is promised to consumers changes at that moment. Do not read a DEFECT row as a fixed date; read it as a hazard that is currently live.

knownLossy.headline: An array of objects does not survive the round trip.
knownLossy.statement: This is the most common shape in real data - order line items, event attachments, CDC row images - and under default configuration it comes back wrong. Elements are duplicated, elements are deleted, or the array is rebuilt as an object keyed by index. A two-element array of objects at the document root does round-trip, and so does any array whose path is named explicitly to JsonReconstructor.arrayPaths(...) with inferArraysFromValues(false); nothing else in this corpus does. Treat arrayPaths as mandatory, not optional.

knownLossy.headline: An array of scalars turns its parent object into an array.
knownLossy.statement: A list of strings one level below the root does not come back as a list of strings inside an object: the containing object itself is reconstructed as a JSON array. At the document root an array of scalars never reconstructs at all.

knownLossy.headline: An empty object, an empty array and an explicit null are the same value afterwards.
knownLossy.statement: {} and [] and null all flatten to null and all reconstruct as null. Three distinct authored values arrive as one. If your schema distinguishes "no items" from "field not set", this library cannot carry that distinction. The nesting DEPTH of an empty chain is preserved, which means you get keys back with no leaves under them.

knownLossy.headline: A non-finite number is indistinguishable afterwards from a string of the same text.
knownLossy.statement: Two separate facts, split because only one of them was previously backed by a fixture. (a) A literal that overflows a double during PARSING becomes the text "Infinity" - vd-exponent-overflow-and-underflow records a genuine Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY going through the flattener's isInfinite branch. (b) A non-finite Double handed to flatten() by a Spark Row is byte-identical afterwards to a user string of the same text - vd-nonfinite-double-collides-with-its-text. JSON has no NaN literal, so (b) was unassertable until the typed input hatch existed.

knownLossy.headline: An integer past Long.MAX_VALUE stops being a number and becomes a quoted string.
knownLossy.statement: The digits survive exactly - nothing is truncated and no value wraps negative, which an earlier version of this library did do - but the JSON type changes from number to string. Anything downstream that type-checks before parsing will reject it.

knownLossy.headline: Declared decimal scale is destroyed, and the flag that claims to prevent that cannot fire on the JSON stack.
knownLossy.statement: 37.7740 comes back as 37.774; an 18-digit FX rate is rounded to a double. preserveBigDecimalPrecision keeps exact text when you hand MapFlattener a real BigDecimal, but the JSON stack parses fractional numbers to Double before the flattener ever runs, so on that stack the flag is inert. Do not carry money through this library as a JSON number.

knownLossy.headline: Field names made of underscores collide with the library's internal markers and are silently deleted.
knownLossy.statement: A field named ___ is dropped outright - no exception, no warning, no null placeholder (NP-022). The whole __*__ namespace is swallowed, including entire subtrees beneath it, which takes out the __meta__ and __type__ headers that event envelopes routinely carry. A field named __isArray__ converts its parent object into a JSON array. An empty-string key is renamed to empty_key and overwrites any real sibling of that name.

knownLossy.headline: Anything whose serialised text starts with a bracket is turned into an array.
knownLossy.statement: The collision class is wider than a string that merely looks like an array, and it is two classes rather than one. THREE members are BYTE-IDENTICAL and two pair invariants assert it: a genuine array, a scalar string containing array text, and a byte[] all flatten to exactly S:[1,2,3] - the last of them with no string and no array anywhere in the input. Object[] and Set belong to the class only in the weaker sense that they too become bracket-leading strings and retype their parent as a list; they carry different element values, so they are pinned by vd-object-array-and-set-become-array-text's own recording and by no byte-equality pair. Whichever one you fed in, the parent object is retyped as an array on the way back. This previously read "all flatten to the same bracket-leading value", which a reader of the neighbouring byte-identity invariant would have taken for byte identity of all five.

knownLossy.headline: ArraySerializationFormat.COMMA_SEPARATED invents arrays out of ordinary strings.
knownLossy.statement: A comma anywhere inside a scalar string - a product description, an address - makes that string reconstruct as an array. Element types are coerced, and an empty or trailing-null element is lost entirely rather than merely retyped. This format is not safe for free text.

knownLossy.headline: The naming strategies restructure the document rather than only renaming fields.
knownLossy.statement: SNAKE_CASE injects unescaped separator characters, which turns a flat scalar field into a nested object on the way back. The case-collision disambiguator emits an unescaped _2 that the decoder reads as another level of nesting. The same field name is sanitised differently at the root than deeper down, so one name yields two column names. UPPER_CASE is the one strategy that renames without damaging the encoding. NARROWED IN 2.1.0 for the disambiguator only: the corrupted structure it used to produce - {"id":{"2":2,"_value":1}}, a numeric-string key beside a fabricated _value, from the two scalars {"Id":1,"id":2} - is no longer returned. The reconstructor now refuses the key set with KeyCollisionException ([BL-023]). The PRODUCER is unchanged and is filed as [BL-024]: generateUniqueKey runs AFTER encoding and appends a raw separator, so the strategy is still emitting a key it cannot round-trip. Loud rather than corrupting is an improvement, not a repair.

knownLossy.headline: maxDepth, maxArraySize and maxMapSize discard data with no marker, no warning and no exception.
knownLossy.statement: Past maxDepth the subtree is replaced by its JSON text, which is indistinguishable from a user string that happens to contain that text - the corpus pins that collision as a pair invariant. Past maxArraySize the extra elements are gone. Past maxMapSize the trailing fields are gone. maxArraySize=1 does not shorten the array, it changes the reconstructed type from array to object, so a resource bound silently rewrites your schema. maxDepth(0) is the one bound that fails closed, at configuration time.

knownLossy.headline: preserveNulls(false) erases present nulls, and a ragged array turns an absent field into a present null.
knownLossy.statement: Absent-key versus present-null is preserved by default and is one of the guarantees this corpus does make - but turning preserveNulls off voids it silently, and inside an array of objects a field missing from one element comes back as an explicit null on that element.

knownLossy.headline: A mixed-type array produces a key set the reconstructor cannot represent, and since 2.1.0 it says so instead of guessing.
knownLossy.statement: A mixed-type array emits a base-key column beside the extracted field columns - mixed and mixed_a - and mixed is then both a leaf and an intermediate path of mixed_a. No JSON node is a scalar and an object at once, so one side cannot be represented. REWRITTEN IN 2.1.0, and the behaviour it describes changed with it. BEFORE: the outcome was decided by the iteration order of the flattened map, silently. Objects before the scalars and the object elements were deleted; scalars first and the flattener's internal _value marker was fabricated into the reconstructed document as if it were a value. Same two entries, two structurally different documents, no exception and no log at any level. NOW: the colliding keys are found before any write, as a set intersection that cannot depend on order, and reconstruct refuses with KeyCollisionException naming the key, every longer key it shadows, and the escaped form that would have disambiguated. The _value wrapper is deleted outright. A caller who would rather keep going can choose a side by name with JsonReconstructor.builder().onKeyCollision(PREFER_LEAF | PREFER_BRANCH); both drop the same side every time and log at WARN. WHAT IS STILL LOST: the source is still not reproduced. The correct answer exists - the base column and the field columns are two columns of ONE array and zipping them by outer index recovers the document - and it is not implemented. The FLATTEN side is not at fault and its column name was deliberately NOT renamed; see [BL-022]. Note the collision also arises with no mixed-type array anywhere: an optional nested object inside an array of records produces it from pure user data.

knownLossy.headline: An Avro union takes the first branch that will accept the value and coerces to it.
knownLossy.statement: A string branch listed before int turns every value in that field into text. [long, double] truncates a fractional value to an integer. For a union of records, the first branch sharing any field name wins and the remaining data is dropped. A nullable string whose value is the literal text "null" comes back as an actual null. NARROWED IN 2.1.0 for one position only: inside an ARRAY ELEMENT, a union of three or more branches used to be dropped entirely - the field became null with no log at any level - and is now resolved by a real index-aware branch selector, or refused by name when two record branches match the same columns. The top-level first-branch-wins behaviour above is UNCHANGED; avro-union-of-records-overlapping-fields is still DEFECT. NARROWED FURTHER IN THE SAME RELEASE, after review measured that the first version of that array-element selector had itself become an instance of this very entry. It tried the branches in DECLARATION ORDER, so a value that was a STRING in the source document was coerced into an earlier numeric or boolean branch even though the flattener had NOT erased its type at that position - the JSON column keeps the quotes, items_meta=["0007"], and Jackson boxes the element as a String. Measured: "0007" under ["null","int","long","string"] came back as Integer 7, "hello" under ["null","boolean","string"] came back as Boolean false because Boolean.parseBoolean never throws, and "1e999" under ["null","double","string"] came back as Infinity. Selection inside an array element is now TYPE-DIRECTED first and declaration order second, so a String prefers STRING/ENUM/BYTES/FIXED, a Number prefers the numeric branches and a Boolean prefers BOOLEAN; a branch carrying a logical type is never demoted. Where the value's Java type has no branch to prefer the coercion is unavoidable, still happens, and now logs a WARN naming the before and after text. NONE of this reaches the TOP-LEVEL union, and the distinction is the reason: there the flat map holds meta=0007 as a bare unquoted scalar, so the type genuinely has been erased and any choice is a guess. NARROWED AGAIN IN 2.1.0, and this time the repair was in the FLATTENER, not the reconstructor: avro-array-element-multi-branch-union-mixed-branches used to sit in this list and is now LOSSLESS, so it has been removed from it. Its residual fault was never union resolution at all - MapFlattener built each array-element column by APPENDING values as it met them and then tail-padding to the longest column, so a column first seen at element k landed at index 0. items_meta came out as [plain, null] when element 1 was the one carrying 'plain'. Columns are now written by INDEX, the misalignment is gone, and both elements resolve to their own branch.

knownLossy.headline: One null element destroys an entire Avro array of records.
knownLossy.statement: A single null inside an array of records annihilates the whole array, and one null nested record erases the nested records of every other element in that array. NARROWED IN 2.1.0: a third loss used to sit here unlisted because no fixture reached it - an array whose element fields ALL live inside a nested record silently returned ONE element instead of N, under every array format including the JSON default. That is repaired and pinned by avro-array-of-records-nested-only-collapses-to-one. Disagreeing column lengths, which used to be reconciled by padding the short columns and duplicating the last nested value, now throw ArrayCardinalityException; the corpus cannot express that input, so it is pinned in AvroArrayOfRecordsSizingTest instead. AND ONE MORE, caught in review before release: the format-driven column split that repaired the collapse above introduced the SAME collapse in the opposite direction at the SHIPPED DEFAULT. Under arrayFormat=JSON an UNBRACKETED delimited column returned one element holding the raw concatenated text - {items_sku=S1,S2,S3} became one record rather than three - with no exception and no log of any level. MapFlattener's JSON writer always brackets a column, including a single-element one, so such a column cannot have come from it; it now raises ArrayFormatMismatchException naming the configured format, the format that would read the data, and how many records the other reading finds. The guard fires only where the two readings disagree, so an unbracketed column with no delimiter in it is left alone. AND ONE MORE NARROWING IN 2.1.0, in the flattener: the array LENGTH is no longer lost. orders now comes back with its true two elements rather than collapsing to one, because array-element columns are written by index instead of appended and tail-padded. The record data is still annihilated, so the row stays DEFECT; only the count is now honest.

knownLossy.headline: Avro schema flattening erases logical types, field defaults, and enum and fixed identity.
knownLossy.statement: Every logical type on a field inside an array becomes an untyped STRING column. Field defaults are gone from the reconstructed schema. A fixed-backed decimal loses precision and scale and arrives as uninterpretable bytes. reconstructOriginalSchema never reads its flattenedSchema argument at all - it replays definitions stored during the forward pass, so it will reproduce an original schema even when the flattened schema has thrown the information away. The flattened SCHEMA and the flattened ROWS disagree on column names for any field containing an underscore.

knownLossy.headline: Two controls do not do what their names say.
knownLossy.statement: useArrayBoundarySeparator marks no array boundaries; it is a global rename of the separator from _ to __, and switching it on collapses __ inside field names and manufactures collisions that did not exist. strictKeyValidation performs no validation and rejects nothing; it silently rewrites names, and three distinct names can fold into one column. A THIRD LEFT THIS LIST IN 2.1.0: AvroReconstructor.allowMissingFields allowed a missing field at neither value - it only selected which exception you got - and now fails with the flattened path at false and substitutes the Avro type default at true, refusing where no type default exists.

knownLossy.headline: Three settings are wired, documented, readable - and cannot change the output.
knownLossy.statement: JsonReconstructor.maxDepth and MapFlattener.preserveBigDecimalPrecision on the JSON stack were the first two, and MapFlattener.detectCircularReferences is the third: it has no effect on a self-referential List, because the visit-stack calls exist only on the object path. Each is proven inert by a probe that measures the two settings producing byte-identical output. A FOURTH was listed here until now - FlattenOptions.inheritDoc, which was read nowhere in src/main - and it has been repaired rather than merely documented: it is now honoured, its probe expects the two settings to DIFFER, and its row is published LOSSLESS as enriched-inheritdoc-false-reports-declared-only-docs. A FIFTH was found and repaired in the same breath in 2.1.0 and so never joined this list: AvroReconstructor.arrayFormat was live for leaf arrays and provably DEAD for arrays of records - all four settings produced byte-identical output on a document built to reach that branch - because the split ran in a static method that could not read the instance field. avro-array-of-records-pipe-format-comma-inside-element is the row that would have gone red had it existed, and now holds.

knownLossy.headline: reconstruct() returns an Avro record that cannot be written.
knownLossy.statement: AvroReconstructor has two data entry points and they do not agree. reconstructToMap returns a Map and is what the LOSSLESS Avro rows are about. reconstruct returns a GenericRecord, and it rebuilds only the ROOT record: every nested record, array element and map value is left as the raw LinkedHashMap the map-building step produced. The builder validates nullability and nothing else, so build() succeeds, the object looks correct in a debugger, GenericData.validate returns false and writing it throws ClassCastException in an executor. REPAIRED IN 2.1.0 AND NO LONGER PART OF THIS LOSS - the second cause this entry used to describe: the ROOT record itself failed validate whenever the schema had a defaulted ENUM, FIXED, BYTES or null field absent from the input, at the SHIPPED DEFAULT configuration and with no nesting involved, because useSchemaDefaults(true) set Field.defaultVal() and JacksonUtils returns the JSON shape (a String for an enum, byte[] for FIXED/BYTES, the JsonProperties.NULL_VALUE singleton for a null default). Defaults now go through GenericData.getDefaultValue, deep-copied, so the root record validates and encodes. What survives is the NESTING: a RECORD-typed default is correct leaf-by-leaf in reconstructToMap and is still handed back as a LinkedHashMap by reconstruct(), because mapToGenericRecord is one level deep. The empty-flattened-map disagreement is also gone - both entry points now fail identically, naming the field - so that fixture has left this list.

knownLossy.headline: A self-referential schema kills the task rather than failing the record.
knownLossy.statement: AvroSchemaFlattener walks a schema with neither a visited set nor an open-type set, so a record containing itself exhausts the JVM stack in the first pass. The failure is a StackOverflowError, an Error, so ordinary per-record error handling does not catch it and the Spark task dies. EnrichedSchemaFlattener refuses the same schema with a typed RecursiveSchemaException naming the cycle, which is the correct behaviour and is why that pair is the argument for the new API.

knownLossy.headline: The cached schema factory identifies a schema by its name, not its content.
knownLossy.statement: getFlattenedSchema(Schema) memoises in a process-wide static map keyed on the schema's full name plus two flags. Flatten two versions of the same named record in one JVM and the second silently receives the first's columns, and the instance's record definitions are left describing the first, so the schema inverse replays it too. In a long-lived executor a registry version bump is discarded for the JVM lifetime.

knownLossy.headline: The enriched schema API names columns your rows do not have, and its defaults are deliberately not the flattener it replaces.
knownLossy.statement: Under its default collision policy EnrichedSchemaFlattener emits field names verbatim while MapFlattener escapes them, so the StructType it describes and the rows the library produces disagree on every field containing the separator. Its defaults also differ from GAvroSchemaFlattener's names on two independent axes - escaping, and the array-boundary marker - and that is now a deliberate choice rather than a broken promise: the parity claim has been withdrawn from the defaults, and FlattenOptions.gAvroParity() reproduces GAvro's names for callers migrating, at the cost of emitting backslashes that are illegal in Avro and SQL identifiers. PARITY IS SCOPED, NOT UNCONDITIONAL, and the page used to say otherwise: it holds for record-rooted schemas that avoid a union with more than one non-null branch, an array of arrays of records, depth past 50, and a non-record root. On the first two a whole subtree collapses to one leaf - GAvro yields payload_k and grid_v where the parity preset yields payload and grid - so the column is missing rather than renamed and no configuration reaches it; both are now measured. The depth divergence is measured nowhere and is prose on the factory's javadoc. The ESCAPE policy is INJECTIVE but NOT DECODABLE: the array-boundary marker is emitted outside the escaped alphabet, so splitting a rendered name yields a phantom empty segment at every boundary - use pathSegments() and arrayBoundaries(), never the name. NO TWO EMITTED COLUMNS SHARE A FLATTENED NAME, under either policy and for injected columns as well as source ones: a boundary marker an ordinary field name can spell is refused, and so is a name supplied through injectField() that another column already holds. THREE WARNINGS THAT USED TO STAND HERE HAVE BEEN REPAIRED and their rows are now LOSSLESS: stream() no longer discards configured column injections that flatten() honours, a producer property whose name collides with an Avro structural attribute at a different position is no longer dropped, and inheritDoc(false) no longer returns inherited documentation. TWO MORE OUTPUT-SIDE GUARDS WERE REPAIRED THAT NO WARNING EVER STOOD FOR, because no fixture could see them: injectField() bypassed the collision guard under both policies, so an injected name equal to a source column's returned two columns of one name even under FAIL, and maxFields bounded only the leaves the traversal visited, so maxFields(2) with two injections returned four columns. The first now has a row of its own; the second is covered by unit test only, because the corpus has no assert mode that can see a field-count ceiling.

knownLossy.headline: Every Java value that is not a String, Number or Boolean leaves this library as a String.
knownLossy.statement: Stack A's declared input is Map<String,Object> and Spark supplies Date, Instant, UUID, enum constants, byte[], Object[], Set and non-String map keys through it. All of them are erased, none is marked, and the library offers no inverse. java.util.Date is worse than erased: it is flattened via Date.toString(), which formats through the JVM default timezone, so the flattened value is not a function of its input and two executors in different regions emit different data. A non-String map key is stringified and, on collision, renamed to a field name nobody wrote.

knownLossy.headline: The cycle guard marks Map cycles and misses List cycles.
knownLossy.statement: detectCircularReferences defaults on and works: a self-referential Map is cut with an explicit marker rather than hanging. It does nothing for a self-referential List, because the visit-stack calls exist only on the object path, so the list case is bounded by maxDepth alone and emits nested brackets around a JDK toString artefact with no marker at all. Neither marker is escaped, so both are aliasable by data a user could legitimately have authored.

knownLossy.headline: The code on this page was, until now, free text that nothing compiled and nothing ran.
knownLossy.statement: Every stack recipe published here is now the body of a compiled method, extracted from source and asserted byte-identical, and each one is executed against a corpus row and compared to that row's recording. That gate found two live faults in what this page previously published: the JSON recipe could not compile at all, because JsonFlattener's constructor is private and, at 2.0.0, no public member returned the type (2.1.0's Builder.buildFlattener() has since changed that, but the recipe was already corrected and is unaffected); and the Avro recipe named a statically cached factory that no measurement in the corpus had ever executed and that returns another schema's columns when a name repeats. EVERY row publishes holdsUnderPublishedRecipe - not a third of them - and the number that say NO is the derived figure in the summary table and in section 5. It is deliberately not written out here: for as long as it was prose this sentence said 25 against a measured 24, on the same page as the generated line that said 24, and no gate could tell.

classificationOverrides.reason: MEASUREMENT OVERRIDES THE PREDICTION. Predicted ACCEPTED_LOSS on the grounds that the JSON integer -0 loses its sign. It does - but at Jackson parse time, before flatten() is called, so it is absent from the baseline as well as from the result and no part of the round trip under test destroys it. The IEEE-754 double -0.0 is preserved end to end and the MAP arm pins it (rendered via Double.toString, so -0.0 and 0.0 stay distinct). Declared LOSSLESS for the round trip, with the parse-time integer loss recorded as out of scope.

MEASUREMENT OVERRIDES THE PREDICTION. Predicted DEFECT on the grounds that reconstruction throws. It does not: Avro's own DecimalConversion normalises scale with RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY, so 12.5 becomes 12.50 exactly and both fields encode correctly. What survives is the exact numeric value at the declared scale; what changes is the Java representation, from Double to the ByteBuffer the schema mandates. That is an accepted representation change, not a fidelity defect. The two residual faults this datum does NOT reach are recorded in the fixture and are unfixtured gaps.

DELIBERATE CLASSIFICATION CHANGE, not a measurement disagreement. The designer filed this ACCEPTED_LOSS while stating in the same breath that the fixed-decimal half is a DEFECT and should be split out. It cannot be split without changing the fixture count, so the aggregate label must reflect the worse half. Enum-to-string is genuinely accepted: SQL and Spark have no enum type and the symbol text is a faithful projection. Fixed-decimal-to-bare-bytes is not: precision 18 and scale 4 are gone and the eight bytes are uninterpretable by any consumer of the flattened schema.

DELIBERATE RECLASSIFICATION, ACCEPTED_LOSS -> DEFECT, on review of the loss claims. The fixture was filed as an accepted delimiter collision while its own detail said the reconstructor 'fabricates extra rows and duplicates values' and called that not defensible. The measurement is worse than the label: a two-line order reconstructs as FOUR line items, with SKU-312 repeated three times and quantity 8 attached to two lines that were never ordered. Losing the comma inside 'Bolt, hex, M8' is an accepted consequence of asking for a comma-delimited format; inventing two billable order lines is not, and publishing it under a classification whose repair status reads 'not scheduled for repair' would be indefensible. This follows the precedent already set by avro-enum-accepted-fixed-decimal-erased: where a fixture straddles both categories, the aggregate label must reflect the worse half.

DELIBERATE RECLASSIFICATION, ACCEPTED_LOSS -> DEFECT, on review of the loss claims. This row and vd-integer-past-long measure the identical behaviour - a BigInteger past Long.MAX_VALUE is emitted as a quoted string, every digit intact and the JSON type gone - and the corpus was publishing them under different classifications, so the same fact appeared to a consumer as a defect under repair in one family and an accepted design limit in another. The stated rationale, 'exact-but-retyped beats silently-wrong', compares the behaviour to the older implementation that wrapped to a negative number; that is an argument for why it is no longer a catastrophe, not an argument for why it is correct. The manifest text already conceded it was 'still open and worth separate triage'. Aligned with vd-integer-past-long as DEFECT.

PREDICTED LOSSLESS, MEASURED LOSSY. The design reasoned that a subtree truncated by maxDepth round-trips as the JSON text it was truncated to. It does not: the baseline is the ORIGINAL nested object, so a_b comes back as a string where the source had an object, and truncation is lossy by construction. Published ACCEPTED_LOSS to match depth-one-over-max, which is the identical mechanism at a different bound. The row still does the job it was built for - it is the purpose-built NO case for holdsUnderPublishedRecipe - but its LOSS is not an independent finding and the detail says so.

DELIBERATE RECLASSIFICATION, DEFECT -> ACCEPTED_LOSS, with the recording unmoved. The fixture's prediction was correct and is left standing: the enriched defaults do not reproduce GAvroSchemaFlattener's names, and every byte of the measurement is unchanged. What changed is the promise. FlattenOptions' javadoc claimed parity FOR THE DEFAULTS; that claim is withdrawn, because meeting it would mean making ESCAPE the resting state and emitting backslashes into names destined to become Avro and SQL identifiers. A documented, deliberate, configure-around-able difference between two flatteners' conventions is an accepted limit, not a defect - and the way round it, FlattenOptions.gAvroParity(), is now real and is measured by the twin row enriched-gavro-parity-factory-matches-gavro-on-underscored-names on the same schema and datum. Kept as an override rather than by rewriting the prediction, following the precedent of order-line-items-comma-separated: where the measurement has not moved and only the judgement has, the disagreement is the honest record. SCOPE, ADDED ON REVIEW: 'configure-around-able' is true of THIS row's shape and is not true in general, and the page used to publish it without the qualifier. gAvroParity() is exact only for record-rooted schemas that avoid four structural divergences no configuration can express: a union with more than one non-null branch, an array of arrays of records, depth past 50, and a non-record root. The first two are now measured - enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-a-multi-branch-union and enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-an-array-of-arrays-of-records - and on both of them a whole subtree collapses to one leaf, so the column GAvro produces is not reachable here under any configuration at all.

DELIBERATE RECLASSIFICATION, DEFECT -> ACCEPTED_LOSS, with the recording unmoved. The phantom empty segment is still there and the fixture still predicts it; what has been withdrawn is NameCollisionPolicy.ESCAPE's claim to be 'lossless and reversible', which described a decoder this package never shipped. The guarantee is narrowed to the one that is true and useful - injectivity - and the rest of the package already said the rendered name must not be parsed (PathSegment's javadoc, FlattenedField.sourcePath(), arrayBoundarySeparator()); this one javadoc sentence was the outlier. fixtures.title: Pure object chain, depth 8, scalar leaf
fixtures.detail: Flattens to the single key l1_l2_l3_l4_l5_l6_l7_l8 = "leaf". No prefix is flagged as an array because the leaf does not start with a bracket; buildHierarchy rebuilds all 8 levels.

fixtures.title: Top-level array of two homogeneous objects
fixtures.detail: Flattens to users_name = "[\"Alice\",\"Bob\"]" and users_age = "[30,25]". Prefix users sees two serialized values of parsed size 2, is flagged as an array, and reconstructArray zips the columns back into two elements.

fixtures.title: Single-element array of objects - the array-vs-scalar ambiguity
fixtures.detail: Both the array wrapper and the value types are lost. Flattens correctly, but both columns parse to size 1, fail the > 1 test, so users becomes an object path and the leaves are never parsed.

fixtures.title: Objects inside an array inside an object, default config
fixtures.detail: Flatten is correct. analyzeStructure attributes the whole key value to every prefix, so both order and order_items are flagged as array paths, and the enclosing object becomes an array of identical elements while the real array becomes an object of raw text.

fixtures.title: Same nested shape, rescued by explicit arrayPaths with inference off
fixtures.detail: With inference disabled only the configured path order_items enters analysis.arrayPaths; order stays an object path and the array rebuilds exactly.

fixtures.title: Arrays of scalars at the document root never reconstruct
fixtures.detail: Both arrays survive flattening intact and come back as those same Strings. The information is fully present in the flattened form; only the reconstructor discards it.

fixtures.title: Array of scalars one level down turns its parent object into an array
fixtures.detail: Prefix user sees a size-2 serialized array and is flagged as the array path, so the object becomes a 2-element array and the array becomes a scalar at every position.

fixtures.title: Array of arrays, including an empty inner array, at depth
fixtures.detail: Flattening is correct via the _value sentinel. On reconstruct, prefix grid is flagged and the outer object is turned into an array of objects, transposing one nesting level away.

fixtures.title: Nested array mixed with a scalar - the base key is the contract, the collision is refused
fixtures.detail: FLATTEN IS CORRECT AND UNCHANGED. The sentinel column is emitted under the base key "data" at both emit sites, deliberately: [BL-022] traced that a _value suffix would produce the SAME key as a user field literally named `value` and REFUSED the rename. {data, data_name} is an injective encoding of two columns of ONE array; the positional half was repaired in 2.1.0 ([BL-018]), so data_name=[["A"],null] describes outer position 0 and data=[[null],"text"] position 1. Since [BL-023] the reconstruct side REFUSES this document with JsonReconstructor.KeyCollisionException, naming the colliding key, the longer keys it shadows and the escaped form that would have disambiguated. Before 2.1.0 it returned {"data":[[null],"text"]} - data_name annihilated with no exception and no log, and only because the live flat map happens to yield data_name first; the reverse order produced a different document. This row stays DEFECT: a refusal is deterministic and loud, but it still does not reproduce the source. The repair that would make it LOSSLESS is zipping the base column with the field columns by outer index, which is not implemented.

fixtures.title: Heterogeneous array, scalars before the object - internal sentinel leaks out
fixtures.detail: The mirror of heterogeneous-array-object-first: identical key set, opposite insertion order. Before 2.1.0 the leaf arrived first, so setNestedValue wrapped it as {"mixed":{"_value":"[1,2,null]","a":"[null,null,3]"}} - a literal _value key in user output that appears in no source document and that does not survive a re-flatten (the node re-encodes to mixed_\_value, not to mixed). The wrapper is DELETED in 2.1.0, not kept as a fallback: it was reachable only from this collision and it silently duelled with a genuine field named _value. Since [BL-023] the reconstruct side REFUSES this document with JsonReconstructor.KeyCollisionException, naming the colliding key, the longer keys it shadows and the escaped form that would have disambiguated. Stays DEFECT.

fixtures.title: Heterogeneous array, objects before the scalars - object elements silently deleted
fixtures.detail: The one-segment key `mixed` is also an intermediate path of `mixed_a`, so the two cannot both be represented. Before 2.1.0 the longer key's subtree was silently overwritten and the array came back as [null, null, x, y] with both object elements deleted - no exception, no log, and the winner decided by whichever key the map yielded last. Since [BL-023] the reconstruct side REFUSES this document with JsonReconstructor.KeyCollisionException, naming the colliding key, the longer keys it shadows and the escaped form that would have disambiguated. This row and heterogeneous-array-scalar-first are the same defect in opposite orders and used to record structurally different documents; they now record the same refusal, which is the point. Stays DEFECT: the source is still not reproduced.

fixtures.title: A user field named value beside the sentinel - the two columns a _value suffix would have fused
fixtures.detail: THE MEASUREMENT THAT REFUSED THE [BL-022] RENAME. joinEncodedKey extends an already-encoded path without re-escaping it, so a user field literally named `value` produces the segment `value` and the key mixed_value. Under the proposed _value suffix columnFor would hand back the SAME column for the sentinel and for the field, fusing element 0's field value with element 1's bare scalar into one mixed_value=[1,"x"] with no way to tell them apart - a loss at FLATTEN time, where nothing downstream can undo it. TODAY, recorded here: mixed_value=[1,null] beside mixed=[null,"x"], two distinguishable columns, nothing lost. Reconstruct then hits the same [BL-023] collision as every other row in this family and refuses. DEFECT for the reconstruct half only; the flatten half is the guarantee this row exists to hold.

fixtures.title: A nullable nested record inside an array of records - the collision with NO sentinel anywhere
fixtures.detail: THE ROW THAT REFUTES THE FRAMING OF [BL-022]. Decoding every flat key in the corpus into segment lists finds EIGHT rows where one key is a strict prefix of another, and only FIVE involve a flattener sentinel. This is one of the three that do not: {"orders":[{"id":1,"ship":{"city":"NY"}},{"id":2,"ship":null}]} is ordinary user data - an optional nested object present in one element and null in another - and it emits orders_ship, a leaf column created purely by the null, beside orders_ship_city. Before 2.1.0 reconstruct returned {"orders":[{"id":1,"ship":null},{"id":2,"ship":null}]}, deleting the nested record from a completely ordinary document with no exception and no log. Since [BL-023] the reconstruct side REFUSES this document with JsonReconstructor.KeyCollisionException, naming the colliding key, the longer keys it shadows and the escaped form that would have disambiguated. Its AVRO twin, avro-array-of-records-nullable-nested-record-shadowed, already existed; the JSON and MAP stacks had no row at all, which is why the collision looked like a sentinel problem for six passes. Stays DEFECT.

fixtures.title: Array of objects with a missing field - absent becomes present-null
fixtures.detail: The second element gains a key it never had. Array length, ordering and all present values are correct, so only a key-set comparison catches it.

fixtures.title: Array of objects whose elements contain a nested object - elements duplicated
fixtures.detail: Both people and people_addr are flagged as arrays from one value; index 1 falls into the use-last-value fallback and reuses the same nested holder, so LA is replaced by a duplicate of a wrong value.

fixtures.title: Empty object, empty array and explicit null at depth, plus an empty chain
fixtures.detail: Three distinct container states collapse to one null. The ACCEPTED half holds: nesting depth of the empty chain is preserved exactly.

fixtures.title: useArrayBoundarySeparator ON: index-like keys and an array of objects
fixtures.detail: Semantically identical to the flag-OFF run - only the character count of the keys differs.

fixtures.title: useArrayBoundarySeparator ON mangles a field name containing __ and collides with its sibling
fixtures.detail: sanitizeKey rewrites a__b to a_b; the genuine sibling then collides and generateUniqueKey renames it a_b_2. One field silently renamed, the other given an invented numeric suffix, no error and no warning.

fixtures.title: Flattener maxDepth reached mid-document - subtree preserved as verbatim JSON text
fixtures.detail: Re-nesting below the limit is lost; the content is not. The reconstructor leaves the truncated String alone because looksLikeSerializedArray requires a leading bracket.

fixtures.title: Field names matching the reconstructor internal marker syntax are silently deleted
fixtures.detail: Flattening is correct and lossless; processArrays then drops both __meta__ and ___ by the marker-skip test. No error, no warning, no count discrepancy reported anywhere.

fixtures.title: Strings that impersonate JSON literals stay strings, and stay distinct from the literals
fixtures.detail: Every value is a String, Boolean or Number that normalizePrimitive returns unchanged. No value promotes the wrap prefix to an array path. QUALIFIED: this row's flattened output is byte-identical to vd-nonfinite-double-collides-with-its-text, which authors three of the same fields as real Doubles - NaN and the two infinities - and does NOT round-trip. The pair invariant pair-nonfinite-double-collides-with-its-text asserts that equality, so the claim that a genuine string "NaN" must not acquire a non-finite tag is now enforceable in both directions rather than only one.

fixtures.title: Every integer boundary up to Long.MAX_VALUE survives with its exact type
fixtures.detail: Jackson yields Integer for the small values and Long for the rest; normalizePrimitive returns any Number untouched, so 9007199254740993 comes back exactly.

fixtures.title: One integer past Long.MAX_VALUE stops being a number and becomes a quoted string
fixtures.detail: i64max survives as a number; i64maxPlus1 and huge are parsed as BigInteger, hit longValueExact, and fall back to decimal text. No digit is lost; the TYPE is.

fixtures.title: Declared decimal scale and beyond-double precision are destroyed before the flattener ever runs
fixtures.detail: Declared scale is gone on trailingZero and oneFive; highScale drops to double precision; beyondDouble becomes indistinguishable from the literal 1.0. The exact digit strings are Jackson/JDK details - if measurement differs, correct the literal, not the classification.

fixtures.title: preserveBigDecimalPrecision is wired, readable, documented - and cannot fire on the JSON stack
fixtures.detail: Output is byte-identical to the same run with the flag false. The probe proves the flag has zero observable effect on this stack. The LIVE side is now a first-class row rather than a field inside this probe: vd-bigdecimal-java-native-scale-loss-and-the-live-flag hands MapFlattener a real BigDecimal through the typed javaInput hatch and its probe measures the two flag settings producing DIFFERENT output. This row's BIGDECIMAL_TWIN probe is now partly redundant with that one and is KEPT deliberately: it is the JSON-stack fixture's only way to reach a Java type, and javaInput is MAP-only.

fixtures.title: A finite JSON number silently becomes the string "Infinity", and a tiny one becomes exactly zero
fixtures.detail: over/negOver overflow to Infinity and are emitted as JSON strings; under underflows to 0.0; nearMax survives with exponent reformatting only. This row DOES reach a genuine Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY through normalizePrimitive's isInfinite branch - the MAP arm records it - so the Infinity half of the non-finite warning is pinned here. It cannot reach NaN: JSON has no literal for it and the corpus's lenient mapper does not enable ALLOW_NON_NUMERIC_NUMBERS. vd-nonfinite-double-collides-with-its-text is the row that reaches NaN, through the typed javaInput hatch.

fixtures.title: IEEE-754 negative zero survives; the JSON integer -0 does not
fixtures.detail: negDouble keeps its sign bit; negInt loses its minus sign. Defensible: no Java integral type can represent a signed zero and preserving it would require promoting every -0 to a double.  ||  MEASURED: CORRECTION. The designer marked this JSON-only on the grounds that the MAP stack cannot observe the integer arm. Measurement shows the JSON stack cannot observe EITHER arm, so as declared the fixture was vacuous: the integer sign is gone at Jackson parse time so it is absent from the baseline as well as the result, and the double sign is invisible under exact-decimal comparison because BigDecimal has no signed zero (both -0.0 and 0.0 render as 0.0). Widened to BOTH. The MAP arm is now the live one: it renders Double.toString, so -0.0 and 0.0 stay distinct and the fixture goes red the moment reconstruction normalises the sign away. Measured LOSSLESS, not ACCEPTED_LOSS: the integer -0 is lost before flatten() is ever called, which is a property of JSON parsing and not of the round trip under test.  ||  CLASSIFIED: MEASUREMENT OVERRIDES THE PREDICTION. Predicted ACCEPTED_LOSS on the grounds that the JSON integer -0 loses its sign. It does - but at Jackson parse time, before flatten() is called, so it is absent from the baseline as well as from the result and no part of the round trip under test destroys it. The IEEE-754 double -0.0 is preserved end to end and the MAP arm pins it (rendered via Double.toString, so -0.0 and 0.0 stay distinct). Declared LOSSLESS for the round trip, with the parse-time integer loss recorded as out of scope.

fixtures.title: Exponent notation is not preserved, and that is fine - this fixture calibrates the oracle
fixtures.detail: The three fractional spellings converge on one canonical form; the integer stays an integer. Nothing about the VALUE is lost.

fixtures.title: The empty-container collapse, followed all the way to the reconstructed JSON document

fixtures.detail: An object becomes an array and the __isArray__ field vanishes. Attacker-controlled key names can change the reconstructed JSON type, which is a schema-inference hazard, not just a fidelity gap.

fixtures.detail: All five are single unescaped segments and reconstruct verbatim, including the embedded double-quote and the literal newline.

fixtures.detail: Neither source name survives, the first value now sits under the name that belonged to the second, and no warning is emitted. Turning the flag off makes both names round-trip perfectly.

fixtures.title: The same field name gets two different column names depending on its nesting depth
fixtures.detail: Two occurrences of one source name land under two different names, and neither is the original.

fixtures.title: SNAKE_CASE turns a flat scalar field into a nested object
fixtures.detail: A scalar at depth 1 is reconstructed as an object at depth 2. Case-folding is a requested transform and would be ACCEPTED_LOSS on its own; inventing structure is not.

fixtures.title: Names differing only by case stay three distinct fields under AS_IS
fixtures.detail: No escaping is triggered, the collision set is case-sensitive, AS_IS skips transformKeys entirely, and all three round-trip exactly.

fixtures.title: The case-collision disambiguator emits an unescaped _2 that the decoder reads as a nesting level
fixtures.detail: NO SENTINEL IS INVOLVED, and that is what this row is for. transformKeys calls generateUniqueKey AFTER encoding and generateUniqueKey appends a RAW separator, so two case-variant fields fold to one name and the disambiguating suffix becomes the key `id_2`, which the decoder reads as a nesting level. Before 2.1.0 the reconstructor turned two scalars into {"id":{"2":2,"_value":1}} - a numeric-string key and a fabricated _value, neither in the source. Since [BL-023] the reconstruct side REFUSES this document with JsonReconstructor.KeyCollisionException, naming the colliding key, the longer keys it shadows and the escaped form that would have disambiguated. Case folding remains an ACCEPTED consequence of the requested strategy; the unescaped suffix is not, and the PRODUCER is now filed in its own right as [BL-024]. Stays DEFECT until the strategy stops emitting a key it cannot round-trip.

fixtures.title: strictKeyValidation is not validation - it silently rewrites and collides
fixtures.detail: All three fold to one name and the clashes are resolved with invented numeric suffixes. The folding is defensible for SQL-safe identifiers; emitting no mapping, no warning and no exception is not.

fixtures.title: A genuine field named _value stays distinct from the flattener _value sentinel
fixtures.detail: No sentinel comparison matches, because every user-supplied segment carries its escape.

fixtures.title: Underscore names either side of the NP-022 trap all survive - pinning exactly where it starts
fixtures.detail: All four decode to their exact source names; __x fails endsWith, x__ fails startsWith, and _ fails both, so processArrays keeps all of them.

fixtures.title: UPPER_CASE changes names as requested and does NOT damage the encoding
fixtures.detail: Names uppercased, structure and nesting intact, the escaped underscore inside a_b still decoded as part of the name. Defensible because the caller explicitly asked for a name transform.

fixtures.title: Flattened schema and flattened rows disagree on column names for any field containing an underscore
fixtures.detail: The schema names a column no row contains. The DATA assertion passes in isolation, so a corpus that only checks DATA reports this document as fully lossless. MATERIAL NEW FACT: the replacement API reproduces this defect rather than fixing it - enriched-keyset-diverges-from-map-rows shows EnrichedSchemaFlattener under its default FAIL policy emitting the same unescaped names. Unlike the legacy path it HAS a resolution, NameCollisionPolicy.ESCAPE (enriched-escape-policy-agrees-with-map-rows), which the legacy path cannot adopt because Avro forbids backslash in field names. A consumer reading this row alone would reasonably infer the new API is the escape hatch. It is not, by default.

fixtures.title: Collision guard rejects a document the data path round-trips losslessly
fixtures.detail: Refusing is defensible: with a non-escapable separator the flattening is genuinely non-injective and silently overwriting one field would be worse. What is not defensible is the asymmetry - the data half round-trips this exact datum with perfect fidelity. There are now FOUR answers to "is this document representable", not two: AvroSchemaFlattener throws, MapFlattener escapes and succeeds, EnrichedSchemaFlattener under FAIL throws (enriched-fail-policy-refuses-a-colliding-schema), and under ESCAPE it escapes and agrees with the rows (enriched-escape-resolves-the-collision). The library still has no single answer; it now has four.

fixtures.title: Array-statistics columns silently swallow a real field of the same name
fixtures.detail: The declared field is dropped and the surviving column is the synthetic statistics one. Assert on the doc string, not merely on the presence of the name, or the fixture cannot tell the two columns apart.

fixtures.detail: Handed an unrelated, field-less record as the flattened schema, the method still returns the original schema. The argument is inert.
