fixtures.title: Field default values are erased by schema reconstruction
fixtures.detail: The reconstructed schema reports no default where the original had one. The DATA path is unaffected, so the loss is confined to the schema half.

fixtures.title: Control: nullable scalars and the six supported logical types round-trip exactly
fixtures.detail: Each logical type reaches convertLogicalType with a value already in its epoch-integer encoding and takes the identity fast path; the uuid is already canonical. The int/long split matters - do not normalise numeric types in the comparator. The reconstruct() half of this row is MEASURED rather than assumed: avro-logical-type-datum-is-writable-control takes THIS ROW'S OWN avsc and datum - all six logical types, every one of them wrapped in a nullable union - through the GenericRecord entry point, and the datum both validates and encodes. This row carries no nested record, which is the condition under which that entry point works. CORRECTION, recorded rather than quietly repaired: the word MEASURED was false when first published. The twin then carried a three-field schema covering two of these six logical types and wrapping none of them in a union - the distinguishing feature of this row - so the conclusion was inferred from a neighbour that did not share the shape. The twin was repointed at this row's own schema and document; the word was not softened.

fixtures.title: A nullable string whose value is the text "null" reconstructs as null
fixtures.detail: status and padded both reconstruct as null; safe survives, which is what lets the fixture distinguish "the sentinel fires too eagerly" from "all strings are broken". No configuration disables this.

fixtures.title: Multi-branch union: a string branch listed before int converts every value to text
fixtures.detail: Both values come back as Strings. No member ordering makes both directions correct - the defect is the absence of a branch discriminator, not the ordering.

fixtures.title: Union [long, double] silently truncates a fractional value to an integer
fixtures.detail: amount reconstructs as an integer with the fraction gone, silently, with no exception anywhere. count is included so the fixture can distinguish "truncates fractions" from "always picks long".

fixtures.title: Union of records: the first branch sharing any field name wins and the rest of the data is dropped
fixtures.detail: The wrong branch is selected and two children go unconsumed. Total silence: no exception, and a structurally valid record of the wrong type. STILL DEFECT - the branch-selection fault is untouched by 2.1.0, because BL-014's repair is confined to the ARRAY-ELEMENT path and this field is on the top-level record, which goes through reconstructUnionValue.  ||  RE-RECORDED IN 2.1.0: the losing branch's defaulted field now comes back as a real Java null. It used to come back as org.apache.avro.JsonProperties.NULL_VALUE, a singleton OBJECT, so a consumer testing `value == null` on a defaulted nullable field saw a non-null object of an Avro-internal type; the corpus rendered that as the AVRO_NULL_DEFAULT token and this row is where it was first measured. That half was filed here for triage as 'useSchemaDefaults should materialise Avro's null default as a real null' and is the NP-023 repair: every schema default now goes through GenericData.getDefaultValue rather than Field.defaultVal(). The avroDoc moved from {"payment":{"brand":"AVRO_NULL_DEFAULT","id":"S:p-1"}} to {"payment":{"brand":null,"id":"S:p-1"}}; routing and account are still dropped.

fixtures.title: A conforming bytes-backed decimal fails to reconstruct because only precision overflow triggers rescaling
fixtures.detail: Reconstruction throws. Bytes-backed decimals do not round-trip from JSON-shaped input at all - and the inversion is the part worth recording: only decimals that were already out of range can be processed. Reading the datum with Avro jsonDecoder hides the whole defect, which is why the harness pins the plain-JSON path.  ||  MEASURED: CORRECTION - THE PREDICTED DEFECT DOES NOT REPRODUCE. Reconstruction does NOT throw. Measured output is two ByteBuffers holding unscaled 1250 and 50, i.e. exactly 12.50 and 0.50 at the declared scale 2. The reason is that Avro itself normalises scale: Conversions.DecimalConversion.validate() calls setScale(declaredScale, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY) whenever the value scale differs, and 12.5 -> 12.50 is exact. The precision-based guard in convertDecimal is therefore dead code for this input rather than a live fault, and the fixture is reclassified ACCEPTED_LOSS: the value survives exactly and the ByteBuffer is the representation the schema mandates. TWO RESIDUAL FINDINGS THIS DATUM DOES NOT COVER, both needing their own fixture: (1) a value with MORE decimal places than the declared scale still reaches Avro with RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY and throws, and the precision guard cannot help because it tests the wrong property; (2) when precision genuinely overflows, the guard rounds HALF_UP silently, so the only decimals this code alters are the ones it should reject.  ||  CLASSIFIED: MEASUREMENT OVERRIDES THE PREDICTION. Predicted DEFECT on the grounds that reconstruction throws. It does not: Avro's own DecimalConversion normalises scale with RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY, so 12.5 becomes 12.50 exactly and both fields encode correctly. What survives is the exact numeric value at the declared scale; what changes is the Java representation, from Double to the ByteBuffer the schema mandates. That is an accepted representation change, not a fidelity defect. The two residual faults this datum does NOT reach are recorded in the fixture and are unfixtured gaps.

fixtures.title: Every logical type on a field inside an array becomes an untyped STRING column
fixtures.detail: The declared decimal precision and scale are unrecoverable from the flattened schema. The DATA assertion on this same datum passes, so only SCHEMA can see the loss.

fixtures.title: Enum to bare STRING is defensible; fixed-backed decimal to bare BYTES is not
fixtures.detail: The enum half is ACCEPTED - SQL and Spark columns have no enum type and the symbol text is the only faithful projection. The fixed-decimal half is a DEFECT and is filed here only because a single classification is required; it should be split if the cap allows.  ||  CLASSIFIED: DELIBERATE CLASSIFICATION CHANGE, not a measurement disagreement. The designer filed this ACCEPTED_LOSS while stating in the same breath that the fixed-decimal half is a DEFECT and should be split out. It cannot be split without changing the fixture count, so the aggregate label must reflect the worse half. Enum-to-string is genuinely accepted: SQL and Spark have no enum type and the symbol text is a faithful projection. Fixed-decimal-to-bare-bytes is not: precision 18 and scale 4 are gone and the eight bytes are uninterpretable by any consumer of the flattened schema.

fixtures.title: A bytes payload literally starting with a Base64 marker is decoded; a fixed value with a high byte fails on platform charset
fixtures.detail: The literal ASCII payload is replaced by decoded bytes with no diagnostic, and the fixed value throws a size mismatch on a UTF-8-default JVM while the same fixture would PASS on an ISO-8859-1-default JVM. A fixture whose outcome depends on file.encoding is exactly what a corpus must pin.  ||  MEASURED: PARTIAL CORRECTION. The fixed/charset half reproduces exactly: reconstruction throws "Fixed size mismatch at sig: expected 4, got 5" because the high byte encodes to two bytes under the JVM default charset (UTF-8 on JDK 18+). The B64 half is NOT observable in this datum: reconstructRecord processes fields in schema order and aborts on sig, so payload is never converted and the sentinel misinterpretation cannot be seen in the output. The fixture pins one of the two defects it was designed to pin; the B64 sentinel needs its own datum with no fixed field beside it.  ||  RE-RECORDED IN 2.1.0, STILL DEFECT. The charset-dependent Fixed reconstruction is NOT repaired - only better described. The size-mismatch message now ends '[decode strategies: bare-base64:invalid; hex:wrong-length-or-not-hex]', which names which of the five decode strategies were attempted and why each declined. Two of those five decline WITHOUT throwing - Strategy 3 can Base64-decode successfully and then discard the result for being the wrong length, and Strategy 4's pre-check can fail on length or charset class - and neither used to leave any trace at all, which is how execution reached the raw-platform-bytes fallback unobserved. This row's own cannotCatch asks for a datum where that fallback SUCCEEDS with the right length and returns fabricated bytes in silence; that case now emits a WARN naming the declined strategies, and still needs its own fixture.

fixtures.title: Control: map with record values, LOSSLESS as a Map only
fixtures.detail: Both keys escape and decode correctly. The result is a HashMap where the input was a LinkedHashMap, but Avro maps are unordered and key insertion order is genuinely not part of the value here. QUALIFIED on the same terms as the array control: reconstruct() returns a record whose map VALUES are LinkedHashMaps, so validate fails and the datum cannot be written. That is asserted, not assumed by analogy - see avro-map-of-records-datum-unwritable, which uses byte-identical avsc and input and differs only in which sibling entry point is called. CORRECTION, recorded rather than quietly repaired: when this qualification was first published that twin carried a DIFFERENT schema (a one-field Attr) and a DIFFERENT document (keys a and b, neither containing the separator), so the sentence above was false and the requalification was exactly the argument by analogy it declared itself not to be. The twin was repointed at this row's own schema and document; the sentence was not softened.

fixtures.title: Control: array of records with a required nested record, LOSSLESS as a Map only
fixtures.detail: Lossless as a Map through reconstructToMap: there is no bare array key, so the array node is not a leaf, the column-wise path is taken, and elements come back in order. QUALIFIED, and the qualification is the important half: the GenericRecord that reconstruct() returns for this same document is NOT a writable datum. Its elements are LinkedHashMaps, GenericData.validate returns false and a binary encode throws ClassCastException. See avro-array-of-records-datum-unwritable, which uses byte-identical schema and input and differs only in which sibling entry point is called. Read this row as a guarantee about reconstructToMap and about nothing else.

fixtures.title: A single null element destroys the records in an array, though no longer its length
fixtures.detail: The record element is still lost - orders comes back [null, null] with the extracted id silently discarded and no exception at any point - so this row stays DEFECT. THE ARRAY LENGTH IS NO LONGER LOST: since 2.1.0 the flattener emits orders_id as [1,null] and orders as [null,null], so the array reconstructs with its true two elements instead of collapsing to one. That is a smaller lie than before, not a repair: a caller who checked the element count would have caught this and now will not, while the data loss that matters is unchanged. The residual cause is the bare base column shadowing the child column, which this repair does not touch.

fixtures.title: One null nested record erases the nested records of every other element
fixtures.detail: The array length is right, the ids are right, and the nested record content is gone from every element. Silent, no exception, plausible-looking output.

fixtures.title: Nesting one level below maxDepth expands fully
fixtures.detail: Two map levels, deepest flattenObject runs at depth 1, no truncation; neither value triggers array inference.

fixtures.title: Nesting at exactly maxDepth expands fully
fixtures.detail: Three map levels, deepest flattenObject runs at depth 2, the check does not fire, and the exact three-level structure rebuilds.

fixtures.title: Nesting one level past maxDepth stringifies the subtree instead of expanding it
fixtures.detail: Bounding depth necessarily truncates, and embedding the exact JSON text is the least-destructive truncation available: every byte survives. What is not defensible is that the type change carries no marker.
fixtures.configDescription: MapFlattener.builder().maxDepth(3); flat map must equal depth-overflow-aliases-a-real-string

fixtures.title: A genuine JSON-text string at maxDepth is byte-identical to a truncated subtree past maxDepth
fixtures.detail: This document alone round-trips exactly. The defect is that its flattened form is byte-identical to depth-one-over-max, and the paired assertion is what records it.
fixtures.configDescription: MapFlattener.builder().maxDepth(3); flat map must equal depth-one-over-max

fixtures.title: At one structural position, maxDepth truncates the map and spares the list
fixtures.detail: Sibling keys at the same nesting position get opposite treatment, and reconstruction then compounds it by inferring an array and duplicating the stringified map into an element it never occupied.

fixtures.title: An empty map at the depth limit is admitted where a non-empty map is truncated
fixtures.detail: Two sibling values at the identical structural position, one exempt from the bound and one not: {} becomes null without consulting maxDepth while the non-empty sibling is stringified.

fixtures.title: Deeply nested empty chains: three keys from a document with no leaves at all
fixtures.detail: Zero leaves in, three keys out. Depth is preserved exactly - the already-pinned ACCEPTED behaviour - but every {} became null, the already-pinned DEFECT, now shown to propagate at every depth.

fixtures.title: A three-element array of maps under maxArraySize=4 round-trips exactly
fixtures.detail: limit = min(3,4) = 3, no truncation, all columns the same length so no padding occurs and the zip-back is exact.

fixtures.title: An array of exactly maxArraySize elements is not truncated
fixtures.detail: limit = min(3,3) = 3, all elements retained, identical behaviour to the below-max fixture.

fixtures.title: An array one element past maxArraySize loses the extra element silently
fixtures.detail: Discarding elements past a configured array bound is precisely what the bound is for, and critically the TYPE survives - the field is still a list of the right element shape.

fixtures.title: A sparse array under the array-cell budget is untouched
fixtures.detail: A sparse array well under the cell budget. Four cells against a budget of eight; the bound never fires and the output is byte-identical to the default configuration.

fixtures.title: A sparse array exactly at the array-cell budget is permitted
fixtures.detail: The boundary from below. Two columns of two slots is exactly four cells and exactly the budget, so the comparison must be > and not >=. An off-by-one here turns a documented ceiling into a ceiling minus one, and nothing notices until a legitimate document at the published figure starts failing.

fixtures.title: A sparse array one cell over the budget is refused, not truncated
fixtures.detail: The boundary from above, and the whole reason the bound exists. Four cells against a budget of three is REFUSED, not truncated, and the refusal names the column, the running total and the knob to move. Truncation was rejected deliberately: dropping columns past a budget leaves every surviving column exactly the right length, so no downstream length check - not ArrayCardinalityException, not agreedElementCount - could see that whole fields had vanished. That is the defect class of the 2.1.0 alignment repair, and a refusal is the only outcome that cannot be silent.

fixtures.title: maxArraySize=1 does not shorten the array, it turns it into an object
fixtures.detail: An array of three objects comes back as an object with string fields: element type, container type and value type all wrong. Set maxArraySize to 2 and the same document returns a proper array - two configurations of one bound, two different reconstructed schemas.

fixtures.title: A one-element array round-trips to a string even with limits wide open
fixtures.detail: Flattening is exactly right; reconstruction fails on arity alone. At arity 1 the array degrades to a string while at arity 2 the PARENT is wrongly promoted, so no single-sided fix resolves both.

fixtures.title: Sparse array of maps: cells grow quadratically, and every element gains nulls it never had
fixtures.detail: HALF OF THIS ROW WAS REPAIRED IN 2.1.0 AND THE TITLE CHANGED WITH IT. The relocation is gone: r_k2 is now [null,2,null] and r_k3 is [null,null,3], so each sparse value sits under the element that carried it. What survives, and keeps this row DEFECT, is the other half: every element gains an explicit null for every key it never had, so element 0 comes back as {k1:1, k2:null, k3:null, z:0} where the source document had only {k1:1, z:0}. Absent and present-null are indistinguishable on the way back, and no marker exists to tell them apart. The quadratic cell growth is also unchanged and is now unconditional: one column per distinct field across all elements, each column pre-sized to the element count. What HAS changed is that the product is now bounded: maxArrayCells (default 1,048,576, per flatten() invocation) refuses a document that would exceed it, so "nothing bounds the column count" stopped being true in 2.1.0. This row is far below the bound and is unaffected by it; the three array-cells-* rows carry the boundary.

fixtures.title: A 210-field record under a single parent round-trips exactly
fixtures.detail: Every value fails the String check so no array inference runs and the record rebuilds field-for-field.

fixtures.title: Separator-laden field names at width: the NP-021 blow-up shape, now expected to be linear
fixtures.detail: The literal underscores inside the names are escaped and the structural ones are not; decodeSegments recovers exactly three segments per key.

fixtures.title: A record wider than maxMapSize loses its trailing fields
fixtures.detail: Capping record width is the stated purpose of maxMapSize, iteration order is deterministic so the truncation is reproducible, and nothing about the surviving data type or position changes. One inconsistency worth recording: this bound announces itself at WARN while the array bound announces itself only at DEBUG.

fixtures.title: JsonReconstructor.maxDepth(2) happily reconstructs eight levels
fixtures.detail: The document round-trips perfectly under maxDepth(2), and the probe proves the setting is inert by showing maxDepth(1) and maxDepth(1000) produce byte-identical results. FlattenOptions.inheritDoc used to be cited here as the corpus's second dead control, in a different subsystem; it has since been wired up and its row publishes LOSSLESS as enriched-inheritdoc-false-reports-declared-only-docs, so this one now stands with vd-preserve-bigdecimal-flag-inert and circular-list-reference-escapes-the-guard. Operational note: the flattener converts StackOverflowError to IllegalStateException while the reconstructor catches only Exception.
fixtures.configDescription: JsonReconstructor.builder().maxDepth(2); probe compares maxDepth(1) against maxDepth(1000) on the identical flat map

fixtures.title: maxDepth(0) is rejected at configuration time, before any document is seen
fixtures.detail: Throws IllegalArgumentException during configuration - the input document is never parsed or flattened. Failing closed is right: a depth budget of zero has no coherent meaning and both alternatives (clamping, honouring) are worse.
fixtures.configDescription: MapFlattener.builder().maxDepth(0) - expected to throw at build time

fixtures.title: E-commerce order with two line items, nested shipping address and an explicit null discount
fixtures.detail: line_items is detected as an array; shipping_address has no array-valued leaf so it stays an object. Both discount_pct slots are physically present in both elements so the padding path is never entered.

fixtures.title: E-commerce order with exactly one line item
fixtures.detail: The array becomes an object AND its leaves become JSON text: both the container type and the leaf types are wrong.

fixtures.title: E-commerce order whose line items each carry a nested ship_from block
fixtures.detail: Warehouse identity is destroyed for both items: the nested block is duplicated across elements and its leaves stay raw text.

fixtures.title: E-commerce order where only the second line item carries a discount
fixtures.detail: THE MIGRATION IS FIXED IN 2.1.0; THE FABRICATED NULL IS NOT. discount_pct now stays on line item 2 (SKU-205) where the document put it - previously it was applied to line item 1 (SKU-100), silent financial corruption that round-tripped with a correct field count and a plausible shape. What keeps this row DEFECT is that line item 1 still gains an explicit discount_pct of null that it never carried. A consumer cannot tell 'no discount was recorded' from 'a discount of null was recorded'.

fixtures.title: Abandoned cart with no line items, no promo codes and an uncomputed totals block
fixtures.detail: A consumer iterating line_items now has to null-guard a field the source schema declares as a non-nullable array.

fixtures.title: Order whose line items each carry a tag array of differing length
fixtures.detail: Element identity and count are right; the tags type is wrong - inner arrays degrade to JSON text and one nesting level is lost.

fixtures.title: Order with two top-level arrays of plain strings
fixtures.detail: Both arrays come back as JSON strings. Flattening is correct; the single-segment keys never enter the prefix loop, so inference is never offered the path.

fixtures.title: Order exported in COMMA_SEPARATED format with a description containing commas
fixtures.detail: Defensible because the format exists to feed CSV/Athena SERDEs that cannot represent an embedded delimiter, the collision is documented verbatim, and a lossless alternative is one builder call away. NOT defensible, and worth separate triage: the reconstructor fabricates extra rows and duplicates values rather than reporting that the element counts disagree.

fixtures.title: Customer profile with two addresses, a preferences map and non-ASCII names
fixtures.detail: addresses is detected as an array; preferences holds only scalars and booleans so it stays an object. The postal code survives as a String because serializeArray writes it with JSON quotes.

fixtures.title: Customer profile carrying both a preferences object and a legacy flat preferences_theme column
fixtures.detail: The nested path encodes to two segments joined by the separator while the literal legacy field encodes to one segment with the separator escaped; decodeSegments splits only on unescaped separators.

fixtures.title: Customer profile whose preferences map contains a notification_channels array
fixtures.detail: preferences becomes a three-element array with the scalars duplicated. Genuinely ambiguous on the wire, so a correct fix is a format change - but the same class of ambiguity in the KEY domain was treated as a bug worth a breaking change, and the value domain deserves the same verdict.

fixtures.title: Event envelope with a __meta__ header and a __type__ payload discriminator
fixtures.detail: Flattening is faithful; the loss is entirely in the reconstructor internal-marker guard. Correct fix is to stop putting markers in the user namespace, not to tighten the name pattern.

fixtures.title: Event envelope whose attachments array mixes objects with a legacy inline string
fixtures.detail: A realistic event envelope whose attachments array mixes two objects with an inline string. The base key `attachments` shadows both `attachments_kind` and `attachments_url`. Before 2.1.0 both object attachments were silently deleted and the array came back as [null, null, legacy-inline-note]. Since [BL-023] the reconstruct side REFUSES this document with JsonReconstructor.KeyCollisionException, naming the colliding key, the longer keys it shadows and the escaped form that would have disambiguated. The refusal names BOTH shadowed columns, not just the first, so the diagnosis is complete on a single throw. Stays DEFECT: an envelope that used to be processed with two attachments missing is now refused, which is correct and is still not the source.

fixtures.title: Financial transaction with a sub-cent amount, an 18-digit FX rate and money-as-text alongside
fixtures.detail: amount.value and fx_rate lose precision at PARSE time; amount_text survives exactly. Marked JSON-only because on the MAP stack the source Map already holds the rounded Double and the fixture would report LOSSLESS while silently destroying money.

fixtures.title: Financial transaction with an amount in minor units beyond long range, next to a 2^53+1 sequence
fixtures.detail: Exact-but-retyped beats silently-wrong: the alternative it replaced truncated the low 64 bits and produced a plausible NEGATIVE number nothing downstream could detect. Still open and worth separate triage: the flattener could keep the BigInteger, or the reconstructor could re-widen.

fixtures.title: Telemetry record with four-level optional groups, null sensor readings and a sparse label map
fixtures.detail: Every prefix sees only scalars and nulls so none is misread as an array; preserveNulls defaults true so both nulls come back explicit.

fixtures.title: CDC insert event with a null before-image and a populated after-image
fixtures.detail: before reconstructs as an explicit null; source and after are scalar-only so both stay objects; the epoch-millis long is never routed through double.

fixtures.title: CDC update where both before and after images contain a tag_list array of different lengths
fixtures.detail: A downstream diff now compares a 2-row array with a 3-row array and reports every field as changed, when the only real change was status plus one added tag.

fixtures.title: reconstruct() returns a GenericRecord whose nested record is a LinkedHashMap
fixtures.detail: reconstruct() returns a GenericRecord whose nested Ship record is a LinkedHashMap. The rendered document is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the source - the corpus oracle renders a GenericRecord and a LinkedHashMap the same way - so the entire verdict comes from the datum checks: GenericData.validate returns false, the nested path is reported as ship=LinkedHashMap, and a binary encode throws ClassCastException. A round-trip-equality harness alone is structurally blind to this defect.

fixtures.title: The array-of-records control document, taken through reconstruct() instead of reconstructToMap()
fixtures.detail: Byte-identical schema and input to avro-array-of-records-control, which is published LOSSLESS; the only variable is the entry point. orders is set as a list of LinkedHashMaps - BOTH elements, so a fix that repairs only element 0 still fails - validate returns false and the encode throws ClassCastException.

fixtures.title: The map-of-records control document, taken through reconstruct() instead of reconstructToMap()
fixtures.detail: Byte-identical avsc and input to avro-map-of-records-control, which is published LOSSLESS; the only variable is the entry point. attrs{temp} and attrs{hum_pct} are both LinkedHashMaps - BOTH entries, so a fix that repairs only the first still fails - validate returns false and the encode throws ClassCastException. avroDoc equals avroBaseline, so the checksHold conjunction is what makes the row lossy rather than the rendering. Because the document now carries the control's hum_pct key, the row also covers separator escaping on a map key through this entry point, which the schema it previously carried did not.

fixtures.title: Control: a record of scalars survives reconstruct() as a writable datum
fixtures.detail: A record of scalars, including a present-null nullable field, survives reconstruct() as a writable datum: validate passes, no non-record path is reported, and the binary encode succeeds. This is what proves the DATUM mode's three gates can return true, so a false on any other DATUM row is signal rather than a constant.

fixtures.title: The nullable-scalars-and-logical-types control, measured through reconstruct() as well
fixtures.detail: Byte-identical avsc and input to avro-nullable-scalars-and-logical-types-control, which is published LOSSLESS; the only variable is the entry point. All six logical types (timestamp-millis, timestamp-micros, date, time-millis, time-micros, uuid) and the nullable-union wrapping survive reconstruct(): validate passes, no nested value is left as a raw map, and the binary encode succeeds. Four of those six and the union wrapping were unmeasured through this entry point until the row was repointed.

fixtures.title: Bare, non-union logical types through reconstruct(): date and timestamp-millis still encode
fixtures.detail: date and timestamp-millis declared BARE - not wrapped in a nullable union - survive reconstruct(): validate passes and the datum encodes. This is the shape avro-logical-type-datum-is-writable-control used to carry and gave up when it was repointed at its own control's byte-identical schema. It is a row rather than a footnote because union resolution runs BEFORE convertLogicalType, so a bare logical type and a union-wrapped one are different code paths, and deleting the bare one to fix a wording defect would have been a silent coverage loss.

fixtures.title: An empty flattened map: reconstruct() refuses it by name, and the message names the field
fixtures.detail: MOVED DEFECT -> ACCEPTED_LOSS in 2.1.0, and the fixture is doing exactly what its own catchesBugClass promised - it said it would catch 'the empty-map early return being deleted or widened', and the early return was deleted. WHAT THIS ROW MEASURES, corrected after review: it is an assert DATUM row, so it runs reconstruct() and only reconstruct(), and it pins that answer plus its exact message. The bug originally filed was the DISAGREEMENT between the two entry points: reconstructToMap short-circuited an empty flattened map into createEmptyRecord, which consulted neither knob, built no GenericRecord and populated only defaulted and nullable fields, while reconstruct() fed that partial map to mapToGenericRecord and build() threw AvroMissingFieldException on the required id. Same input, two answers about whether it is representable. That agreement is now measured in AvroReconstructorEmptyInputTest, NOT here - this row's earlier title and detail both claimed the corpus pinned it, and the DATUM arm never calls reconstructToMap. The test naming it was ADDED in the same correction: checking where the claim actually lived turned up that it lived nowhere, in three documents at once. What this row does publish is the answer and the message: 'Cannot reconstruct com.example.Req: no value in the flattened input and no usable schema default for required field(s) id.' It is ACCEPTED_LOSS and not LOSSLESS because an empty map genuinely cannot produce a record for a schema with a required no-default field - the loss is in the input, not in the library - and datumChecks are still all false.

fixtures.title: The first Avro row measured under a TUNED reconstructor: matched __ separators, and the defaults arm finally diverges
fixtures.detail: Two measurements in one row. (1) The nested-record defect is ORTHOGONAL to the separator: with MapFlattener and AvroReconstructor both switched to the __ boundary separator the keys split correctly and attrs still comes back a LinkedHashMap, so validate fails and the encode throws ClassCastException. (2) avroDefaultsMatch is FALSE - the first time any Avro row has made that comparison do work. Until this row existed no Avro fixture set config.avro.reconstructor, so on all seventeen DATA and DATUM rows the tuned arm and the defaults arm were the identical call and every one published holdsUnderDefaultReconstruction=YES on a comparison that could not fail. The DATA branch disclosed that in a comment; the DATUM branch did not. A consumer who flattens with the boundary separator and reconstructs with a default AvroReconstructor gets a different answer, and that is now measured rather than assumed.

fixtures.title: A self-referential record kills the task with StackOverflowError, not an exception
fixtures.detail: A record whose nullable field is its own type kills the JVM stack. AvroSchemaFlattener.collectRecordDefinitions recurses with neither a visited set nor an open-type set, so it overflows in the FIRST pass. The failure is a StackOverflowError, an Error: it is not caught by ordinary row-level error handling and it kills the Spark task rather than the record. Category trees, org charts and threaded comments are ordinary shapes and no SCHEMA fixture was recursive before this one.

fixtures.title: Two schemas sharing a full name: the second flattening is silently the first
fixtures.detail: getFlattenedSchema(Schema) caches in a private static map keyed on the schema's FULL NAME plus two flags, with no schema content in the key. Flattening a second version of x.Ev returns the FIRST version's columns - amount is absent - and because computeIfAbsent short-circuits the flatten, the instance's record definitions still describe v1, so the inverse replays v1 too. In a long-lived Spark executor a schema-registry version bump is discarded for the JVM lifetime. This is the only row that exercises the cached factory the published Avro recipe used to name.

fixtures.title: Control: two differently-named schemas through the cached entry point each get their own flattening
fixtures.detail: The same two calls with distinct full names: the cache key differs, both flattenings run, the second carries its own columns and its inverse reproduces its own schema. This is what makes the stale row attributable to the KEY rather than to the mode. fixtures.title: Array of records whose element fields ALL live inside a nested record
fixtures.detail: The shape none of the 29 pre-existing AVRO rows could reach, and the headline repair of 2.1.0. Every other array-of-records fixture carries a scalar column at the ELEMENT ROOT, which is exactly the condition under which the old sizing code worked. Take that scalar away and the array node has no columns of its own, so the count had to come from the child nodes - and determineArraySize only counted a child column whose FIRST value was a String beginning '[[', a test that could never fire for a column already parsed into a List. maxSize stayed 0 and a trailing 'maxSize > 0 ? maxSize : 1' fabricated a size of one. fixtures.title: PIPE_SEPARATED array of records with a comma inside an element value
fixtures.detail: The first row in the corpus to set config.avro.reconstructor.arrayFormat, and it exists because that knob was provably INERT on the array-of-records path: measured on a document built to reach the branch, all four settings produced byte-identical output. The split ran in a static method that structurally could not read the instance field, so it sniffed JSON, then comma, then pipe - and because comma came first, a legal comma inside 'Bolt, hex, M8' was treated as a delimiter under PIPE_SEPARATED. MEASURED BEFORE THE REPAIR: two elements became three, the fabricated third carrying sku="" and quantity=0 invented by handleMissingField and a description of 'M8|Washer' that still contained the real delimiter. MapFlattener's javadoc warns about collisions with the delimiter you CONFIGURED; it promises nothing about the other one. Now LOSSLESS: the configured format is honoured and the split is bracket-aware.

fixtures.title: CONTROL: BRACKET_LIST array of records with a comma inside an element value
fixtures.detail: DECLARED A CONTROL: predicted LOSSLESS before the repair and measured LOSSLESS after, so a green result here is not evidence that anything was fixed. It earns its place beside the PIPE_SEPARATED row by holding the other half of the format boundary. BRACKET_LIST is the format most easily broken by a careless 'honour the configured delimiter' change, because MapFlattener's BRACKET_LIST writer QUOTES and ESCAPES every string and recurses into nested lists - it is not brackets around raw text. During this repair a bracket-aware split without unquoting was tried and returned values with literal backslashes in them; DoublyNestedArrayTest caught it, and this row now covers the same boundary from inside the corpus.

fixtures.title: A three-branch union inside an array element, with its data in a child column
fixtures.detail: reconstructArrayOfRecords had never had a UNION arm at all. Its field dispatch knew three shapes - flat column present, RECORD, ARRAY - and unwrapNullable, its only union handling, collapses only [null,T], so a union of arity three arrived still typed UNION, matched nothing and fell into handleMissingField, which saw a NULL branch and wrote a plain null. MEASURED BEFORE THE REPAIR, both as a JUnit failure and by disabling the new arm and re-recording this very fixture (pre-fix avroDoc: {"items":[{"meta":null,"sku":"S:a"},{"meta":null,"sku":"S:b"}]}): items came back as [{sku=a, meta=null}, {sku=b, meta=null}] while items_meta_src=["web","pos"] sat in the tree unread by anything. A NEVER-IMPLEMENTED GAP, NOT A REGRESSION: unwrapUnion, whose 'first non-null branch at any arity' behaviour looks like the missing piece, had four calls and zero declarations through ef625f2 and a declaration with zero callers after, so it never executed. Now LOSSLESS via a real index-aware branch selector. HONEST NARROWING of the filing, also measured: the SILENT drop needs a null branch in the union; a null-free 3+ union was already loud, because the builder threw on the unset field.

fixtures.title: A three-branch union whose two array elements take DIFFERENT branches - now resolved
fixtures.detail: LOSSLESS since 2.1.0. The id is deliberately left defect-shaped so the history stays legible; precedent is avro-array-element-multi-branch-union-dropped. Element 0 resolves to the record branch via the index-aware nested-record helper, and element 1 falls past the failing record branch to the type-directed STRING branch, so meta comes back as the record {src: web} and as the string 'plain' respectively. fixtures.detail: The enriched flattener names columns order_id and ship_post_code; MapFlattener's rows are keyed order\_id and ship_post\_code, because it escapes every raw field name before joining and the enriched flattener under its default FAIL policy does not. fixtures.title: The enriched API reproduces AvroSchemaFlattener's column names exactly, including the wrong ones
fixtures.detail: The enriched API reproduces AvroSchemaFlattener's column names exactly. Mechanically lossless and substantively bad news: the answer both flatteners give is the one avro-underscore-field-name-column-divergence already publishes as a DEFECT, so the new API inherits the defect rather than fixing it. The row's value is that unilateral repair of either flattener now turns the build red.

fixtures.title: The enriched DEFAULTS deliberately do not reproduce GAvroSchemaFlattener's names for a field containing an underscore; gAvroParity() does
fixtures.detail: RECLASSIFIED DEFECT -> ACCEPTED_LOSS, recording unchanged. FlattenOptions' javadoc used to claim its DEFAULTS reproduce GAvroSchemaFlattener's conventions so a caller migrating starts at parity. They do not: GAvro escapes every segment and the enriched defaults under FAIL escape nothing. The claim has been withdrawn from the defaults rather than the defaults changed to meet it, because ESCAPE emits backslashes that are illegal in Avro and SQL identifiers and this flattener's output becomes column names. What is left is a deliberate, bounded, configure-around-able difference between two conventions - which is what ACCEPTED_LOSS means here. FlattenOptions.gAvroParity() is the migration path and now genuinely produces GAvro's names; the twin row enriched-gavro-parity-factory-matches-gavro-on-underscored-names measures it on this exact schema and datum, so the only variable across the pair is the configuration.

fixtures.title: FlattenOptions.gAvroParity() reproduces GAvroSchemaFlattener's names exactly for underscore-bearing fields
fixtures.detail: The positive half of a pair, and the first row in the corpus that can see a named FlattenOptions FACTORY at all. gAvroParity() used to be an alias for builder().build(), so both rows whose titles named it were measuring the defaults and the factory's claim could not be observed - which is how it rotted. It now sets collisionPolicy=ESCAPE and arrayBoundarySeparator=_, and both arms render [order\\_id, ship_city, ship_post\\_code]. Same schema and same datum as the DEFECT twin enriched-gavro-parity-claim-fails-on-underscores, so the only variable is the configuration. NAMES ONLY, and the agreed names contain backslashes, which are illegal in Avro and SQL identifiers - that is inherited from GAvro and is exactly why FAIL remains the default. SCOPE: gAvroParity() is exact only for record-rooted schemas that avoid four structural divergences no configuration can express: a union with more than one non-null branch, an array of arrays of records, depth past 50, and a non-record root. The first two are now measured - enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-a-multi-branch-union and enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-an-array-of-arrays-of-records - and on both of them a whole subtree collapses to one leaf, so the column GAvro produces is not reachable here under any configuration at all.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs GAVRO_SCHEMA_FLATTENER, preset GAVRO_PARITY

fixtures.title: The enriched DEFAULTS deliberately mark array boundaries with a doubled separator where GAvroSchemaFlattener uses a single one; gAvroParity() matches GAvro
fixtures.detail: RECLASSIFIED DEFECT -> ACCEPTED_LOSS, recording unchanged. The second, independent half of the withdrawn parity claim, isolated on an underscore-free schema. Worth stating precisely, because the obvious reading is wrong: GAvroSchemaFlattener has NO array-boundary marker at all. Its useArrayBoundarySeparator flag globally renames the single separator from _ to __, so it emits _ everywhere by default and __ everywhere when set - and the enriched model, a separator plus a distinct boundary marker, corresponds to neither. The enriched default keeps the visible __ marker because it is a useful convention that FlattenedField.arrayBoundaries() sits alongside. The twin row enriched-gavro-parity-factory-matches-gavro-across-an-array-boundary measures the factory reproducing GAvro's single separator on this exact schema.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs GAVRO_SCHEMA_FLATTENER, default FlattenOptions

fixtures.title: FlattenOptions.gAvroParity() joins array element fields with a single separator, exactly as GAvroSchemaFlattener does
fixtures.detail: The second axis of parity, on an underscore-free schema so the boundary marker is the only variable, and the positive twin of enriched-gavro-parity-claim-fails-at-array-boundaries. Both arms render [items_sku] where the enriched defaults render items__sku. The recorded enrichedOptions pins the factory's exact knobs, so any future drift in gAvroParity() - including 'simplifying' it back into builder().build() - turns this row red rather than quietly restoring the defect. The first two are now measured - enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-a-multi-branch-union and enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-an-array-of-arrays-of-records - and on both of them a whole subtree collapses to one leaf, so the column GAvro produces is not reachable here under any configuration at all.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs GAVRO_SCHEMA_FLATTENER, preset GAVRO_PARITY

fixtures.title: gAvroParity() does not reproduce GAvroSchemaFlattener's names for a union with more than one non-null branch, and no configuration reaches it
fixtures.detail: THE SCOPE OF THE PARITY CLAIM, MEASURED. FlattenOptions.gAvroParity()'s javadoc has always scoped parity to record-rooted schemas avoiding four structural divergences; the published page carried none of that scope, and the two overrides that flipped the parity rows from DEFECT to ACCEPTED_LOSS leaned on the difference being configure-around-able. On this shape it is not. GAvroSchemaFlattener descends into the FIRST non-null branch of a multi-branch union and names its field; this flattener resolves only [null, T] and emits one leaf for anything else, because a union of two records has no column layout without a discriminator. GAvro yields [payload_k], the parity preset yields [payload], and payload_k is unreachable from any FlattenOptions. Filed as an accepted loss rather than a defect because closing it would mean adopting GAvro's silent discarding of every branch but the first.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs GAVRO_SCHEMA_FLATTENER, preset GAVRO_PARITY

fixtures.title: gAvroParity() does not reproduce GAvroSchemaFlattener's names for an array of arrays of records, and no configuration reaches it
fixtures.detail: The second axis of the same scope, and the twin of the union row. GAvroSchemaFlattener digs through the outer array into the inner array's element record; this flattener resolves an array's element type once and emits a single leaf when that element is itself an array. GAvro yields [grid_v], the parity preset yields [grid]. Again a collapse rather than a rename, and again unreachable by configuration. Filed as an accepted loss because closing it would change what withinArray() and arrayBoundaries() mean for every caller of the enriched API, not only for the ones migrating off GAvro.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs GAVRO_SCHEMA_FLATTENER, preset GAVRO_PARITY

fixtures.title: stream() emits the columns injectField() configured, at the same positions flatten() gives them
fixtures.detail: PUBLISHED AS A DEFECT UNTIL NOW, AND REPAIRED: flatten() spliced injected columns in at their positions and stream() returned none of them, with no error and no diagnostic. The javadoc defended that by asserting positional splicing needs the whole sequence in memory, which is false - the merge is monotone over the OUTPUT index and never reads the source length, so it costs one integer plus the injection map the configuration already holds. flatten() is now defined as the materialising form of stream(), so the two cannot diverge by construction. A second divergence nothing had pinned went with it: source fields streamed with their raw source ordinal while flatten() renumbered every field to its final index, so the two entry points disagreed on position() even for the columns stream() did emit. NOTE FOR THE READER: with the two entry points now in agreement by construction, the ENRICHED_STREAM comparator can no longer report 'not equal' under any configuration, so its discriminating power is held by the harness gate RoundTripFidelityCorpusTest.enrichedStreamComparatorStillDiscriminates rather than by a failing row.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs ENRICHED_STREAM, one injected field

fixtures.title: An injection positioned past the last column is appended in ascending order by both entry points, not dropped and not left at its declared index
fixtures.detail: Reaches the append-past-the-end branch that the injection row's own cannotCatch named as unreachable by any fixture. injectField(99, x) against a three-column schema yields column 4 on both entry points - not a dropped column, and not a column at position 99 with a 95-slot gap in front of it. The rule is surprising enough that a caller could reasonably expect either of those, and until now it was documented only in a comment inside a private method; it is now stated on injectField's javadoc.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs ENRICHED_STREAM, one injected field at position 99

fixtures.title: An injected column whose name is already a source column's is refused, rather than returning two columns under one name
fixtures.detail: PUBLISHED AS AN ENFORCED PROPERTY BEFORE ANYTHING MEASURED IT, AND NOW MEASURED. This page said injectivity was enforced rather than assumed; it was enforced only for the columns the TRAVERSAL produced. checkCollision and the maxFields ceiling both lived inside emit(), which the injection merge never passes through, so injectField() reached the caller's sink unguarded: on gov.Row{order_id, amount} with injectField(1, "order_id"), flatten() and stream() both returned [order_id, order_id, amount] under NameCollisionPolicy.FAIL, whose entire published job is refusing exactly that, with no exception and no log line. None of the three existing injection rows could see it because all three inject names disjoint from their source columns. It now throws SchemaFlattenException naming both the source path and the injectField position, in its own text: neither policy's advice - rename a field, change the separator, switch to ESCAPE - can move a name the caller typed. ACCEPTED_LOSS on the same footing as enriched-fail-policy-refuses-a-colliding-schema: the schema half refuses what the row half never faces.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs MAP_FLATTENER, one injected field named after a source column

fixtures.title: Without injections, flatten() and stream() return the same columns in the same order
fixtures.detail: Without injections the two entry points return the same columns in the same order, and the recorded emission order pins the sequence as well as the set. WHAT THIS ROW IS FOR HAS CHANGED, and the rationale it used to publish here is withdrawn as stale: it read 'this is what stops the injection row's comparator being one that has only ever produced not equal', which described the risk before flatten() became the materialising form of stream(). After that repair the risk is the mirror image - the ENRICHED_STREAM comparator can no longer report 'not equal' under any configuration in which both entry points return - so the discriminating power lives in the harness gate RoundTripFidelityCorpusTest.enrichedStreamComparatorStillDiscriminates, which compares stream() with and without injections and now counts refusals and emissions separately so neither arm can quietly become the only one. What this row still pins on its own is emission ORDER, and the zero-injection short circuit in stream(), which is a real and separately reachable code path: it hands the caller's sink to the traversal unwrapped and rebuilds no field.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs ENRICHED_STREAM, default FlattenOptions

fixtures.title: The same recursive schema: the legacy flattener dies with an Error, the enriched one refuses with a typed exception
fixtures.detail: The same recursive schema as avro-recursive-schema-stack-overflows, one variable changed. The enriched flattener checks an OPEN-type deque on the way down and throws RecursiveSchemaException naming the cycle; the legacy flattener exhausts the stack. Accepted rather than defect because a recursive schema genuinely has no finite flattened form, so refusing is the right answer and the loss is bounded and typed. This pair IS the argument for the new API.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs LEGACY_AVRO_SCHEMA_FLATTENER, default FlattenOptions

fixtures.title: Control: on an array-free nested record the two flatteners produce identical columns
fixtures.detail: On an array-free nested record - with the Addr type used twice but never inside itself - the enriched and legacy flatteners emit identical columns. Array-free on purpose: the two disagree on the array-boundary marker, so any array here would fail the control for a reason that is not about correctness. It is also the cheapest detector for guardRecursion regressing from an open-set to a visited-set check.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_KEYSET vs LEGACY_AVRO_SCHEMA_FLATTENER, default FlattenOptions

fixtures.title: Every custom Avro property the producer declared reaches at least one flattened leaf
fixtures.detail: Every custom property the producer declared - two on a field, one on a nested record, one on a nested field - reaches at least one flattened leaf. Compared as a SET, because with inheritance on a record-level property reaches N leaves and a per-path comparison would report divergence for a reason that is a feature; placement is recorded separately and pinned byte-exactly without being the verdict. Its blind spot used to be real and is now historical: it carries only x- property names, so it could not see the private reserved-name filter that dropped a producer property called "size"; the sibling row that could is enriched-reserved-prop-name-collision-drops-a-producer-property, which now publishes LOSSLESS and stands guard against that filter being reintroduced.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_METADATA vs PROPERTY_SET, default FlattenOptions

fixtures.title: A producer property named "size" survives the flatten, because the structural-versus-custom split is Avro's to make and a name list cannot make it
fixtures.detail: PUBLISHED AS A DEFECT UNTIL NOW, AND REPAIRED: a field-level property named "size" is legitimate user metadata that Avro hands over, and the flattener discarded it against a private thirteen-name blocklist while the javadoc four lines above swore nothing was filtered by name. The blocklist is deleted. Avro's parser had already performed the structural/custom split, CONTEXTUALLY: FIELD_RESERVED on a field, SCHEMA_RESERVED on a schema, ENUM_RESERVED on an enum, and logicalType in none of them - so "size" is structural on a fixed schema and ordinary metadata on a record field, and a filter holding only a String cannot distinguish them. Six of the thirteen entries could never match at the field call site and seven destroyed producer metadata. Ten names now survive that did not: namespace, fields, items, values, symbols, size and logicalType on a field, and default, order and logicalType on a record, which inheritance then pushes onto every leaf beneath it. Nothing structural started appearing - Avro's reserved sets are supersets of each position's structural keys.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_METADATA vs PROPERTY_SET, default FlattenOptions

fixtures.title: inheritRecordProperties(false) drops the record-level property from every leaf
fixtures.detail: inheritRecordProperties(false) removes the record-level property from every leaf, so it is absent from the emitted set while still present in the declared one. Exactly what the caller asked for, bounded to record-level properties, and disclosed by requiresNonDefaultConfig. Its probe measures the two settings producing DIFFERENT output. That used to make it the LIVE twin of a DEAD inheritDoc control sitting one line away in the same options class; inheritDoc is now live too, so the two are a matched pair of property-inheritance and doc-inheritance controls, each of which goes red if it falls silent.

fixtures.title: When no ancestor declares documentation, every leaf's reported doc is exactly the doc it declared
fixtures.detail: When no ancestor declares documentation, each leaf's reported doc is exactly the doc it declared and isDocInherited is false. The passing leg of the doc comparator, without which that comparator could only ever report divergence.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_METADATA vs DECLARED_DOC, default FlattenOptions

fixtures.title: A leaf that declared no documentation is reported as documented, with the enclosing record's text
fixtures.detail: Three leaves that declared no documentation are reported as documented, carrying the enclosing record's text. Inheritance is deliberate and isDocInherited is the honest flag, so the loss of provenance is bounded and recoverable - but a consumer does receive, for a column, documentation the producer never wrote about that column, and in a governance pipeline that text propagates into a data dictionary. The remedy now exists and is named: inheritDoc(false) returns declared-only documentation, measured by enriched-inheritdoc-false-reports-declared-only-docs. An accepted loss with an opt-out reads differently from one without, and until that control was wired up there was no opt-out.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_METADATA vs DECLARED_DOC, default FlattenOptions (inheritDoc defaults true)

fixtures.title: FlattenOptions.inheritDoc(false) returns declared-only documentation, attributing nothing to a leaf its producer never documented
fixtures.detail: PUBLISHED AS A DEFECT UNTIL NOW, AND REPAIRED: inheritDoc was declared, defaulted, validated, stored and exposed by a getter, and read nowhere in src/main, so inheritDoc(false) was byte-identical to inheritDoc(true) and a consumer asking for declared-only documentation received inherited documentation with no error and no diagnostic. walkRecord now gates the inherited value at its source: with the flag off, no ancestor text is carried down the walk and every leaf reports exactly the documentation its own producer wrote. The probe now expects the two settings to produce DIFFERENT output, which is what proves the control is live; it previously expected EQUAL, which is what proved it dead. A LEAF'S OWN DOC STILL WINS - the flag suppresses inheritance, not documentation - AND THIS ROW NOW MEASURES THAT RATHER THAN ASSERTING IT: review found every leaf in the schema undocumented, which made the DECLARED_DOC arm satisfied equally by a correct fix and by one that blanket-nulled every doc, so order_id was given a doc of its own and deliberately re-recorded. It survives the flag while the two customer leaves report null, and an erasing implementation now reddens this row on its own recording.

fixtures.title: Under ESCAPE, per-segment escaping of the separator's first character survives a decode when no array boundary is crossed
fixtures.detail: Under ESCAPE, with no array crossed, decoding each flattened name recovers exactly the source path segments. What it really pins is the per-SEGMENT escaping rule - FlattenedPath escapes the separator's FIRST character rather than the complete separator string, a distinction a property test caught once already. It used to be described as the most literal round-trip claim in the enriched API; that claim has been withdrawn from NameCollisionPolicy.ESCAPE, so the decodability here is a CONSEQUENCE of no array being crossed and is explicitly not a guarantee. Its sibling enriched-escape-name-does-not-decode-across-an-array-boundary is the same configuration one array deep.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_METADATA vs DECODED_PATH, collisionPolicy ESCAPE

fixtures.title: An ESCAPE-policy name is injective but not decodable: across an array boundary it splits to a phantom empty segment
fixtures.detail: RECLASSIFIED DEFECT -> ACCEPTED_LOSS, recording unchanged, because the promise moved rather than the behaviour. NameCollisionPolicy.ESCAPE's javadoc claimed the rendering was 'lossless and reversible'. Reversibility is a property of an encode/decode PAIR and this package ships only the encode half; worse, join() escapes each segment against the separator and then joins across an array boundary with a marker emitted OUTSIDE the escaped alphabet, so items__sku still splits to [items, , sku]. The claim is withdrawn and narrowed to what is true and useful: the rendering is INJECTIVE - no two distinct source paths render alike - which is what makes it safe as a map key. Use FlattenedField.pathSegments() and arrayBoundaries() for structure; they carry strictly more than any decoder could recover. And the injectivity half is no longer merely asserted: checkCollision used to return before it checked anything under ESCAPE, on the stated grounds that injectivity held by construction, which was false for a boundary marker an ordinary field name can spell - see enriched-escape-forged-array-boundary-is-refused.
fixtures.configDescription: assert ENRICHED_METADATA vs DECODED_PATH, collisionPolicy ESCAPE

fixtures.title: Under ESCAPE, a boundary marker an ordinary field name can spell is refused rather than emitting the same column name twice
fixtures.detail: Closes a blind spot that let a disabled guard reach an open pull request: no fixture anywhere varied arrayBoundarySeparator under ESCAPE. checkCollision used to return before it checked anything whenever the policy was not FAIL, on the stated grounds that the ESCAPE rendering is injective by construction - true only while the boundary marker is spelled from characters segment escaping escapes, and that setter is free-form. With the marker set to x, a record holding an array a of records with a field b AND a sibling scalar named axb emitted two leaves both called axb, silently. It now throws SchemaFlattenException naming both source paths and the marker. ACCEPTED_LOSS on the same footing as enriched-fail-policy-refuses-a-colliding-schema: MapFlattener keys the same document into two distinct rows, so the schema half refuses what the row half handles - but escaping genuinely cannot separate these two paths, and the alternative is one column name for two columns.

fixtures.title: Instant, UUID and an enum arrive as Strings; Character, Short and Float survive - and nothing marks the difference
fixtures.detail: Instant, UUID and an enum constant all leave the library as Strings; Character, Short and Float survive as themselves. Nothing marks the difference, so nothing downstream can tell an erased UUID from a user string that happens to look like one - the same loss vd-integer-past-long already publishes as a DEFECT. fixtures.title: The flattened value of a java.util.Date depends on the JVM's default timezone, not only on the Date
fixtures.detail: A java.util.Date is flattened by calling Date.toString(), which formats through TimeZone.getDefault(). The column value is therefore a function of ambient JVM state, not only of the data: two Spark executors in different regions emit different values for the same row. The epoch instant also becomes an unparseable English sentence. The corpus pins the zone for the measurement and asserts the pin is restored; that pin is itself the evidence, because a fixture that could not be pinned would be flaky.

fixtures.title: A byte[] flattens to the byte-identical text a real array and an array-lookalike string produce
fixtures.detail: A byte[] never reaches normalizePrimitive: it is diverted to the array path, widened element by element and JSON-serialised, producing the bracket-leading text that a genuine array and an array-lookalike string also produce. The parent object is then retyped as an array AND the binary payload is gone, with none of the base64 marking a ByteBuffer receives. This is the collision class reached with no string and no array anywhere in the input - the type Spark hands you for BinaryType.

fixtures.title: Object[] and a LinkedHashSet are serialized as array text and promote their parent to an array
fixtures.detail: Object[] and a LinkedHashSet are both serialised to array text, both parse back to two elements, and the parent prefix is promoted, so two independent fields are zipped into two synthetic records. These are the last two container types ordinary Java code hands to flatten() that no fixture reached. Set-ness itself is NOT under test - the oracle renders any Collection positionally - and the fixture says so.

fixtures.title: Double.NaN and the string "NaN" flatten to byte-identical output; one round-trips and one does not
fixtures.detail: Three authored Doubles - NaN and both infinities - and three authored Strings of the same text are the same six characters after flattening. The flattened map is byte-identical to vd-string-literal-lookalikes', which is published LOSSLESS, and the pair invariant asserts that equality. JSON has no NaN literal, so this collision was documented in the warning list and unassertable until the typed input hatch existed.

fixtures.title: A real BigDecimal loses its declared scale by default - and preserveBigDecimalPrecision, inert on the JSON stack, is LIVE here
fixtures.detail: A real BigDecimal handed straight to flatten() loses its declared scale under defaults. The probe additionally shows preserveBigDecimalPrecision producing DIFFERENT output on this stack, which is what makes its inertness on the JSON stack (vd-preserve-bigdecimal-flag-inert) a specific defect rather than a general "this option does nothing". requiresNonDefaultConfig is false: the row is measured at defaults and only the probe tunes the flag.

fixtures.title: An Integer key 1 and a String key "1" both stringify to "1"; the second is renamed to a field name nobody wrote
fixtures.detail: An Integer key 1 and a String key "1" both stringify to "1"; the disambiguator renames the second to a field name nobody wrote, which then acquires an escape because it contains the separator. Both the key TYPE and the key IDENTITY are gone and the new name carries no marker. Unreachable from JSON text - every JSON object key is a String - and ordinary from Spark, which hands Map keys of any type for MapType(IntegerType, ...).

fixtures.title: detectCircularReferences is real: a self-referential Map is cut with an explicit marker instead of running away
fixtures.detail: detectCircularReferences is real and this is the only row that can see it: a cyclic graph cannot be expressed as JSON text, so the guard had run unwitnessed on every previous fixture. A self-referential Map is cut with an explicit [CIRCULAR_REFERENCE] marker, and the probe proves the guard is live by measuring detection on and off producing different output. Accepted on the same footing as depth-one-over-max: a cyclic graph has no tree encoding and the library marks rather than hangs. The caveat that must be read with it is that the marker is a bare unescaped string a user could have authored, so this truncation is aliasable exactly as maxDepth truncation is. The marker lands at a_a rather than a because flatten() enters a defensive top-level copy first.

fixtures.title: The same guard does nothing for a self-referential List, and the error path claims otherwise
fixtures.detail: The same guard does nothing for a self-referential List. The visit-stack calls live only in flattenObject, so a List containing itself is bounded only by maxDepth, and the probe measures detection on and off producing IDENTICAL output - the guard is inert here. There is no marker at all: the value is nested brackets around a JDK toString artefact, which is data-shaped and silently wrong, and the sibling Map row shows the library can do better. A guard whose coverage does not match its name.

fixtures.title: A bounded, defaults-holding loss that the published recipe still cannot reproduce
fixtures.detail: maxDepth(2) truncates the subtree below a_b to JSON text, so a_b comes back as a string where the source had an object - the same bounded loss depth-one-over-max already publishes. What is new is the DISCLOSURE: this row holds under default reconstruction (the defaults arm re-reconstructs the fixture's own flattened map and agrees) and does NOT hold under the published recipe, whose flattener runs at its own default depth. That combination is the reason holdsUnderPublishedRecipe exists as a separate column, and this row is the purpose-built proof that it can say NO.

fixtures.title: A plain defaults document is reproduced exactly by the published recipe on both Stack A and Stack B
fixtures.detail: Four scalar runtime types and a present null, at defaults, on both stacks, reproduced exactly by the published recipe. The passing leg of the recipe-verdict drill: without it, a verdict wired to a constant NO would be indistinguishable from a corpus in which no row happens to hold.

pairs.detail: A scalar string holding the text of an array and a genuine array flatten to byte-identical output. THREE members of the class are byte-identical and two pairs assert it: vd-binary-array-collides-with-array-text reaches the same bytes from a byte[], with no string and no array anywhere in the input, and pair-binary-collides-with-array-text holds that equality. Object[] and Set are in the class only in the weaker sense - they become bracket-leading strings and retype their parent as a list, on their own element values rather than these ones - so vd-object-array-and-set-become-array-text is pinned by its own recording and by no byte-equality pair. At most one of the three byte-identical members can ever round-trip without a wire-format change. This equality is the value-domain analogue of the FlattenedPath key-injectivity proof.

A subtree truncated by maxDepth and a genuine user string containing that same JSON text produce the same flattened map. The depth bound output is indistinguishable from ordinary data; a truncation marker would remove the collision, and the day one is added this assertion flips.
At maxArraySize=3 the reconstructed field is still a list. Baseline for the type-flip assertion below.
Truncating from 3 elements to 2 loses data but preserves the container type. This is the well-behaved side of the cliff.

At maxArraySize=1 the same field reconstructs as an OBJECT, not a shorter list. A resource bound has changed the reconstructed schema. Paired with the two assertions above, this names the type flip directly rather than leaving it inside a general inequality.
With every limit wide open, a one-element array still reconstructs as a scalar string. This isolates the size>1 detection gate from maxArraySize entirely.

A byte[] and a string containing array text flatten to byte-identical output. This is the member of the collision class reachable with no string and no array in the input, which is why it cannot be dismissed as a string-parsing quirk.

Deliberately pointed at a published-LOSSLESS row: this LOSSLESS row's flattened output is byte-identical to a document that does not round-trip. The day non-finite doubles are tagged, this equality breaks AND the LOSSLESS row's claim that a genuine string "NaN" must not acquire the tag becomes enforceable in both directions.
The parent of a byte[] reconstructs as a LIST. The binary payload is gone and the container type changed; naming the type flip directly is stronger than leaving it inside a general inequality.
